Advanced packaging revenue, JPY 6 billion in FY March 2026, is now expected at JPY 15 billion in FY March 2027 (Q1 was JPY 4.5 billion) - a significant upward revision from the JPY 6 billion prior plan, driven by both rising customer CapEx and additional POR wins for its film deposition technology. In NAND, demand-supply is not fully adjusted - memory players are allocating clean room to DRAM while NAND wafer output needs to increase - so greenfield NAND investments are expected to resume, which converts all of Kokusai's PORs to sales and is broadly favorable. In DRAM, the D1C transition is complete and D1D is progressing. NAND sales could approach record highs, and DRAM plus NAND plus advanced packaging support growth above WFE (targeting more than a 20% sales increase).
GAA JPY 5 billion in Q1, over JPY 20 billion FY March 2027; advanced packaging raised to JPY 15 billion FY March 2027 from JPY 6 billion in FY March 2026

ADVANCED PACKAGING set a record and contributed nearly one-quarter - 'nearing 25%' - of overall product revenue in Q2, driven by the dimensional metrology portfolio and fuelled by customers' continued investment in advanced packaging and HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY capacity to support AI-related device demand. Nova had guided advanced packaging to between 20 and 25% of product revenue for the year and now sees it 'inching towards the 25% for the year.' Management frames advanced packaging as a MULTI-YEAR STRUCTURAL growth opportunity that has gone from essentially no revenue several years ago to a meaningful contributor, now spanning optical, chemical AND materials metrology, and becoming increasingly similar to front-end manufacturing in complexity across both logic and memory. Chiplets, HYBRID BONDING, PANEL-LEVEL PACKAGING and 2.5D integration all increase both the number of measurements required and their criticality; hybrid bonding is described as 'an additional layer that will accelerate this growth for Nova.'
Advanced packaging a record at nearly 25% of Q2 product revenue, inching toward 25% for the full year (initially guided 20-25%)

The Nova WMC dimensional-metrology platform won a recent TOOL OF RECORD SELECTION BY A LEADING FOUNDRY CUSTOMER (not named on the call) for MULTIPLE LAYERS MEASUREMENT in advanced-packaging production flows. Nova is also seeing accelerating WMC adoption across BOTH memory and foundry customers, 'positioning us to benefit from further investment in advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory manufacturing.' A new configuration of the Nova WMC extends its dimensional metrology capabilities to PANEL-LEVEL PACKAGING.

HBM is one of the two engines behind 30% QoQ growth in the Dragonfly-led inspection business (the other being 2.5D logic): 'For sure, it's HBM, where we've seen really phenomenal growth in both 2D inspection as well as 3D metrology', plus pickup from 3Di and new applications for SUB-SURFACE INSPECTION, which 'becomes more critical for 3D or heterogeneous packaging applications'. Demand across advanced packaging is strongest from HBM MANUFACTURERS and OSATs, driving the full-year advanced-packaging growth outlook up to ~80% (from ~50%). HBM and 2.5D have grown at a similar pace all half, and HBM 'is continuing to be pretty strong' into H2
inspection +30% QoQ on 2.5D + HBM; adv packaging FY26 ~+80%

ADVANCED PACKAGING FULL-YEAR GROWTH OUTLOOK RAISED TO ~80%, up from the ~50% projected just one quarter earlier. Inspection (dominated by Dragonfly) grew 30% QoQ on 2.5D logic AND HBM; advanced packaging + specialty was nearly half of Q2 revenue. Demand is strongest from HBM MANUFACTURERS and OSATs supporting heterogeneous packaging for AI. Headline order: MORE THAN $200 MILLION of Dragonfly orders won from a SINGLE OSAT PARTNER in the quarter, the majority to be delivered in 2027. Growth drivers are the 2.5D expansion at OSATs, HBM (strong in both 2D inspection and 3D metrology), 3Di pickup and sub-surface inspection; the Dragonfly G5 is still a small share of 2026 revenue and becomes a bigger contributor in 2027 (with an ASP lift that feeds gross margin)
adv packaging FY26 ~+80% (was +50%); >$200M single-OSAT Dragonfly order (mostly 2027)

RECORD BACKLOG SURPASSING $1.1 BILLION (roughly double the ~$0.5B last disclosed in Q4). Mix: ~60-70% tied to 2026, ~30-40% covering 2027, described as 'still early'. Management frames it as customers 'confidently issuing purchase orders well in advance of the historical norms' to secure supply slots. Visibility improved MOST in advanced packaging - historically the weaker-visibility segment - because demand is now driven by AI hyperscaler capex rather than consumer end markets; well over half the business comes from advanced packaging. Volume Purchase Agreement (VPA) negotiations for 2027 are just beginning, which should extend visibility further

PANEL-LEVEL PACKAGING revenue expected to MORE THAN DOUBLE year-over-year with further growth in 2027, driven by larger package sizes as heterogeneous packaging adds more die (including silicon photonics). Onto attacks panel from THREE angles: (1) JetStep lithography for LARGE panels (500mm x 500mm square substrates and above), (2) Firefly process control, which now integrates the Dragonfly G5 optics plus Dragonfly metrology sensors - moving panel makers from end-of-line inspection only to in-line process control, and (3) the TSMC CoWoS 310mm x 310mm square-panel path, where packaging process-control technologies already adopted from Onto are being applied. Sold as a suite with Discover Software
panel-level packaging revenue to MORE THAN DOUBLE YoY

→ TSMC: On the panel market: the 310mm x 310mm square-panel path is 'driven through TSMC, that's their CoWoS' - 'a lot of the packaging technologies that they've adopted from us for process control in CoWoS are being applied to CoWoS', spanning inspection and metrology

JAPAN DUAL-TRACK 300MM EXPANSION (METI-supported): TRACK 1 repurposes the Arai facility (ex-Fab 6) for 300mm SILICON PHOTONICS + advanced packaging and maximizes Fab 7 output — FULL PRODUCTION READINESS Q4 2027 (this drives the raised 2028 model; capacity 'already requested by and committed to several lead customers'). TRACK 2 builds a NEW 300mm fab adjacent to Fab 7 for a 4x INCREASE IN JAPANESE 300MM OUTPUT (SiPho, SiGe, advanced optical packaging) — installed and functioning by Q4 2028, the growth path into 2029+; intent to add AT LEAST 20,000-25,000 wpm of SiPho capacity; self-funded, no dilution. Japan chosen for GEOPOLITICAL NEUTRALITY, the Panasonic-heritage R&D workforce, and manufacturing-quality culture.
Track 1: Arai 300mm SiPho ready Q4-2027; Track 2: 4x Japan 300mm output by Q4-2028 (>=20-25k wpm SiPho)

Q1 (Apr-Jun 2026): revenue JPY 123.2 billion with electronics JPY 75.5 billion; operating profit JPY 26.9 billion with electronics JPY 21.4 billion - driven by strong demand for GPU and high-end CPU, stabilized Cell 8 production and improved utilization at existing plants pushing sales volume above the initial plan, plus strong selling prices for high value-added products. First-half forecast raised: revenue to JPY 253 billion (+10%), operating profit from JPY 38 billion to JPY 54.5 billion (+43%), electronics OP from JPY 33 billion to JPY 47 billion (+44%), net profit from JPY 23 billion to JPY 34 billion (+48%).
Q1 revenue JPY 123.2 billion (electronics JPY 75.5 billion), OP JPY 26.9 billion (electronics JPY 21.4 billion); H1 OP forecast raised 43% to JPY 54.5 billion

Full-year FY2026 forecast raised: revenue from JPY 500 billion to JPY 550 billion (+10%), electronics from JPY 350 billion to JPY 375 billion (+14%); operating profit from JPY 90 billion to JPY 127 billion (+41%, operating margin expectation raised from 18% to 23%), electronics OP from JPY 75 billion to JPY 110 billion; net profit raised to JPY 84 billion. Biggest driver: ASP and product mix with a positive impact of JPY 26.5 billion (majority is ASP - the planned quarterly price-reduction curve became less steep or prices were not reduced at all, plus general substrate price increases in an industry-wide supply shortage; not concentrated in a particular customer - GPU, CPU, switching IC and PC ASPs rising across the board). Revenue growth expected in all sub-segments: AI server, switching IC, and general-purpose server/PC.
FY revenue guide JPY 550 billion (from JPY 500 billion); OP JPY 127 billion (from JPY 90 billion, +41%); ASP/mix impact +JPY 26.5 billion

Supply-demand: 'The situation where demand exceeds the industry supply capacity is expected to continue' - substrates are getting larger and more difficult toward next fiscal year and the one after, AI server demand keeps rising, and current selling prices are expected to at least hold at present levels. Customers accepted fewer price cuts, and in some cases none, because of industry-wide shortages. Glass cloth and CCL cost increases are passed through to ASP in a timely manner. Utilization: apart from Intel Cell 5, almost everything was at full capacity utilization; sourcing for the revised FY2026 plan is already secured, though industry-wide competition for materials and equipment could constrain material supply in coming years.
Demand exceeds industry supply capacity; near-full utilization except Intel Cell 5; prices expected to at least hold

Capacity: Cell 6 and Cell 8 are about 50% through equipment ordering, will commence operations within FY2027 with positive business contribution in FY2028 (timing difficult to accelerate). Next investment decision accelerated - to be made at the latest before the end of the current fiscal year; capacity enhancement is needed across the business ('almost all the customers have asked us to enhance our capacity'), with vacant land at Gama and Ono (would-be Cell 7 and Cell 9) both under consideration at the same time, plus possibly buying another plant building. Advance payments from customers continue to be discussed to fund capacity and offset fixed-cost increases; customer stance on advance payments unchanged from the Cell 6 situation despite an aggressive Taiwanese competitor.
Cell 6/Cell 8 ~50% of equipment ordered, operations within FY2027, contribution FY2028; new capacity decision before end of FY2026 (Gama and Ono, Cell 7/Cell 9)

EMIB-T (silicon-bridge embedded substrate): development done by three players including Ibiden, with Ibiden believing it is at the leading edge; a test vehicle has been shipped. Challenges: embedding the silicon bridge in the buildup and getting the interconnection right, plus stronger power supply complicating the core structure (component embedding is a general new trend adding complication) - yield expected lower, but yield has improved a lot since the beginning of development, numbers indicate shippable quality, and there is no showstopper. Small-lot production expected in the latter half of FY2027, mass production at the Gama plant from FY2028.
EMIB-T small-lot production latter half of FY2027; Gama mass production FY2028; yield improving, no showstopper

Glass cloth: procurement risks flagged at the beginning of the year have been mitigated. The number of glass cloth suppliers has increased - previously two companies in Japan and Taiwan, now a third and fourth supplier are visible, giving four glass cloth suppliers with visibility for use in mass production; the Japanese glass cloth supplier is increasing capacity, and the tight glass cloth supply situation is expected to simmer down. Ibiden believes it is in an advantageous position in the industry for glass cloth supply. Glass core substrate: joint development continuing (glass core and component-embedding structures pursued as two separate options with their own roadmaps, possibly narrowing to one later).
Four glass cloth suppliers now visible for mass production (was two); Japanese supplier adding capacity

ARM-based CPU substrates (AI inference CPU demand): specs will be similar to substrates Ibiden currently supplies and difficulty level similar to the AI GPU work, so Ibiden has the capability to supply. New business is capped at around 20% of the overall in FY2027 - there is no room to allocate more capacity, so large-scale initiatives cannot be undertaken despite expected demand; allocation between new business and value-added products of existing customers to be revisited internally by the mid-year earnings call, when the midterm plan will also be revisited.
New business capped at ~20% of overall in FY2027 on capacity limits

→ TSMC: Glass core substrate joint development with TSMC confirmed ongoing ('we are doing the joint development effort. We are working with them'): glass core and component-embedding structures are being pursued simultaneously as two separate options, each with its own roadmap; at some point Ibiden may focus on just one of the two, but for now both developmental efforts continue without preassumption.

→ Intel: Intel Cell 5 is Ibiden's one line not yet at full utilization ('apart from Intel Cell 5, almost everything was at full capacity utilization') and its utilization is improving, driving the sales volume increase from existing capacity. For EMIB-T, Core 5 for Intel will be used for small-lot production (targeted latter half of FY2027) before Gama plant mass manufacturing starts in FY2028.

Advanced Solutions, which includes the Fluxless Thermo-Compression (FTC) bonding platform, recognised revenue 20% ABOVE last quarter's record. K&S is maintaining its target of OVER $100 MILLION in Advanced Solutions revenue for fiscal 2026, and for fiscal 2027 Lester Wong guided TCB revenue to a range of $150 MILLION TO $200 MILLION - significant sequential growth. The company remains closely engaged with a broad base of IDM, OSAT and foundry customers as heterogeneous packaging goes mainstream, with particular confidence in heterogeneous integration around logic for Fluxless TCB.
Advanced Solutions revenue 20% above prior record; >$100M Advanced Solutions target for FY2026; TCB guided to $150M-$200M in FY2027

Beyond thermocompression, K&S accelerated its HYBRID BONDING program over the last year and says its hybrid bonder has unique features not currently in the market; it PLANS TO DELIVER A HYBRID BONDING TOOL TO A CUSTOMER IN THE FIRST HALF OF FISCAL 2027. It is also investing significantly in a PANEL-level project, seeing a lot of interest from IDMs, foundries and OSATs because panel geometry allows many more dies on a rectangle than a circle; specific panel applications are still being scoped with customers. Management frames FTC, vertical wire, direct copper-to-copper, hybrid and panel-based architectures as the emerging packaging set that will be critically necessary across a much wider array of semiconductor production, and stresses the industry is still in the relatively early stages of this More-than-Moore advanced packaging transition.
Hybrid bonding tool to be delivered to a customer in H1 FY2027

Capacity: the Singapore capital expansion is progressing well and remains on track for completion by the FIRST FISCAL HALF OF 2027, supporting Advanced Solutions growth over coming years. For the traditional wire bonding business, K&S has increased capacity FOURFOLD compared with about two quarters ago through its flexible manufacturing model. Management said it is explicitly focused on not losing market share because of capacity constraints, noted K&S has supported $400 million quarters before, and did not see a $450 million quarterly run rate at this point while committing to ramp further if needed.
Wire bonding capacity increased fourfold versus ~two quarters ago; Singapore expansion completing in H1 fiscal 2027

K&S made a notable structural claim about wire bonding in AI infrastructure: it estimates the DATA CENTER MARKET RELIES ON WIRE BONDING TECHNOLOGY AT LEAST AS MUCH AS, IF NOT MORE THAN, traditional semiconductor markets such as smartphones and PCs, because the majority of data center chips are still traditionally wire bonded - general infrastructure, networking, communication, power management and storage. Ball bonding is the more prevalent technology for data center power management, while wedge bonding remains more focused on automotive and high-current applications. Data center expansion therefore drives demand for BOTH the thermocompression and the wire bonding lines.
Kulicke & Soffa states in its fiscal Q3 2026 release that it anticipates its expanded Advanced Solutions production facility will be completed, as scheduled, within the second half of fiscal 2027.

Management reiterates a multi-year growth rate of 30% or a little higher and sees no signs of slowdown in 2027 (AI also lifts TPD, whose business is 70% data center and other AI); timing is moving from a discrete component to integration through chiplets, advanced substrates and modules, which SiTime expects to expand its CED SAM by $2.5 billion by 2030 in opportunities that do not exist today, and the acquisition accelerates the path to $1 billion in revenue.
multi-year growth ~30%; CED SAM +$2.5 billion by 2030

Veeco plans to MORE THAN DOUBLE CAPACITY in advanced packaging and silicon photonics during 2027, expanding internal manufacturing on the East Coast plus strategic outsourcing partnerships with contract manufacturers in Southeast Asia, and adding and training personnel. The company is deliberately spending ahead of revenue in the second half of 2026: approximately $10 million of incremental operating expenses and roughly 75 basis points of full-year gross-margin impact from one-time capacity set-up and contract-manufacturer onboarding costs. This is why the full-year revenue guide rose while the EPS guide came down. The revenue ramp from the optical networking, data storage and advanced packaging orders begins slightly at the end of Q4 2026, starts in Q1 2027 and gets more up to speed in Q2 2027, with the majority falling in 2027.
Capacity in advanced packaging and silicon photonics to more than double during 2027; ~$10M incremental opex and ~75bps gross-margin impact in 2026

Advanced packaging is becoming a materially larger part of the business through the wet processing and lithography portfolio, with demand driven by heterogeneous integration and increasingly complex 2.5D and 3D architectures. Veeco projects the advanced packaging SAM will approach $1 BILLION BY 2030 and expects to gain share within it. The company is actively engaged with a Tier 1 foundry on a PANEL PROCESSING opportunity and is encouraged by the progress. Manufacturing footprint is expanding both in-house and with outsourced partners in Southeast Asia to support the growth.
Advanced packaging SAM approaching $1B by 2030; active panel processing engagement with a Tier 1 foundry

CALL — GUIDE RAISED A THIRD TIME; SUPPLY CHAIN REBUILT: FY2026 revenue raised to ~$12.6B = 40% GROWTH (+$2.1B vs the $10.5B Analyst Day plan, +$1.1B vs May's $11.5B) — the raise deliberately UNALLOCATED across AI fabrics (goal >=$3.5B), campus (>=$1.25B), core front-end data center ('isn't going to be flat' — enterprise, new logos, international) and routing; operating margin RAISED to 48-49% (Q2 hit 49.9%). Supply chain: Jayshree — 'the INDUSTRY is going to have a TWO-YEAR problem... I don't think we get out of it as an industry TILL 2028,' but Arista's specific H1 actions pay off in H2: MULTI-YEAR PURCHASE COMMITMENTS NEARLY TRIPLED YoY to $9.7 BILLION (from $3.6B; $8.9B in Q1); MEMORY SUPPLY SECURED FOR 2026 with visibility WELL INTO 2027 (DDR4/DDR5/NAND); PCB + optics capacity buildable in a 12-month window; a NEW LIQUID-COOLING SUPPLY CHAIN stood up (cold plates, quick disconnects, tubing with capacity agreements); 3 CMs + 3 distribution hubs (US/Asia/Mexico). Price increases only help 'end of the year or more like next year' (backlog); FY GM held 62-64% including memory/silicon cost inflation. Etherlink AI-fabric customers now EXCEED 100 CUMULATIVE (from 4-5 in 2024).
FY26 raised to ~$12.6B (+40%, 3rd raise); purchase commitments ~3x YoY to $9.7B; memory secured into 2027; liquid-cooling chain built; >100 AI customers

Interconnect Solutions (ICS) net sales $685 million, up more than 30% year-over-year and 16% sequentially, organic +28%, led by the three growth platforms of advanced packaging and interconnect, AI PCBs and thermal management, which collectively grew more than 50% year-over-year again; ICS gross margin ~44%, adjusted EBITDA margin ~29%, up 290 basis points YoY, now viewed as structurally in the high 20% range.
ICS $685 million (+30% YoY, +16% QoQ); AI growth platforms +50% YoY; ICS EBITDA margin ~29%

New advanced packaging architectures (panel-level packaging, larger package formats, tighter lines and spaces on high-layer-count boards and IC substrates) all mean more material complexity and more material intensity, with fewer suppliers able to qualify; Qnity has incumbency with the same customers that commercialized the existing advanced packaging formats and expects more content per package as formats grow. Customer capacity expansions in advanced packaging underpin the durability of ICS growth.

Winning new business in pulse plating, a key metallization technology for the most advanced high-layer-count printed circuit boards used in AI applications (density, signal integrity, power delivery); thermal portfolio broadened to liquid thermal interface materials, phase change materials, thermal pads and gap fillers for AI systems and data center infrastructure.

Industry volume indicators: MSI expected in the high single digits for 2026 and PCB growth in the mid to high single digits; Qnity content outperformance sits considerably above the MSI benchmark because all logic and memory leaders are successfully commercializing their most advanced nodes at once.
2026 MSI high single digits; PCB growth mid to high single digits

Pre-payments rose notably in Q2 because GUC pre-buys materials for large CSP turnkey programs - besides CoWoS it must secure HBM stacks and substrate ahead of the build so everything (substrate, HBM, the SoC from TSMC) arrives together for packaging. GUC sells the customer the finished CoWoS package with HBM inside; if HBM prices rise the chip price rises with it, so the cost risk sits with the customer, not GUC. Management cited HBM pricing going from about 240 at the start of the year to 700 and up to 900 (as spoken; unit not stated), fully passed through. Whether HBM procurement flows through GUC's own P&L or is booked as a service fee is still being worked out case by case at this early stage.
HBM price cited from ~240 early in the year to 700-900 (as spoken), passed through to customers

The new Turing design center began trial operation in Q2 running small and mid-size projects and is expected to be in full use in H2; it adds some depreciation/R&D cost but is aimed squarely at 3nm, 2nm and even more advanced process work plus advanced packaging. The R&D roadmap already includes CPO, IVR (integrated voltage regulator), next-generation UCIe die-to-die, and N2-on-N2 advanced-process development; opex should grow only modestly versus a clearly larger revenue increase next year.

LAST QUARTER'S FORECAST DELIVERED EARLY: the sale-of-gas project backlog reached a RECORD $8.1 BILLION (from $7.1B in Q1) — management had guided to exiting 2026 'with an eight handle' — and the 'couple of large electronics contracts' flagged in Q1 landed as $1 BILLION OF NEW ELECTRONICS WINS added to backlog TO SUPPORT THE EXPANSION OF ADVANCED-NODE FABS IN THE WESTERN US. Linde has ALREADY BEGUN CONSTRUCTING those plants under reimbursable letters of intent while the supply contracts are finalized, adding to its existing network of plants in ARIZONA, and says it is pursuing 'a few more large opportunities'. Separately and NOT in the backlog, Linde's TAIWAN JV will invest approximately $800 MILLION to build, own and operate air separation units and HYDROGEN production units supplying NEW SEMICONDUCTOR FABS AND ADVANCED PACKAGING FACILITIES in Taiwan (the Taiwan business is a 50% non-consolidated JV, so excluded from reported numbers). ELECTRONICS IS AGAIN THE FASTEST-GROWING END MARKET, on a combination of project start-ups and 'higher demand tied to hardware associated with AI', and is expected to remain the largest backlog contributor 'for the foreseeable future'.
Record backlog $8.1B; +$1B electronics wins for western-US advanced-node fabs; $800M Taiwan JV (fabs + adv packaging)

Product momentum in FY2027: coater developer (share of more than 90% across EUV to immersion lithography) won PORs in multiple processes in advanced logic and DRAM with the new Resive Pro Dice; full-year etch system sales of JPY 1 trillion are coming within reach; cryogenic etch systems for 400-layer NAND start deploying in customers' mass production lines from calendar 2027; a POR was won for a new low resistance metal deposition system in a new application area. For DRAM interconnect etch, five-year cumulative sales to fiscal 2030 are getting closer to JPY 1 trillion, significantly exceeding the original guidance of JPY 500 billion. In advanced packaging, prober sales show outstanding growth with full-year sales likely to go significantly beyond JPY 100 billion, and the Prexa SDP device prober for advanced logic launched in April; bonder/debonder and 3D-IC are growth areas combining leading-edge front-end and bonding technology.

Coater developer share more than 90%; etch sales JPY 1 trillion full-year within reach; DRAM interconnect etch five-year cumulative sales near JPY 1 trillion vs JPY 500 billion original guidance; prober sales significantly beyond JPY 100 billion; cryogenic etch for 400 layers in mass production from calendar 2027

Record ATM (OSAT) revenue NTD 126.1B (+12% QoQ, +36% YoY) with ATM gross margin 27.3% and operating margin 15.7%; full-year 2026 ATM revenue expected to grow ~35%. Capacity is the binding constraint — blended utilization 80-85% but 'generally very close to being full', with near-term growth gated by equipment installation and building construction. Q4 2026 ATM gross margin is likely to EXCEED the 30% structural ceiling, after which management will review raising the 26-29% structural margin range upward; pricing environment described as friendly, with material and component cost inflation passed through to customers.
ATM record NTD 126.1B (+36% YoY), GM 27.3%; Q4 GM to break the 30% structural ceiling

LEAP (leading-edge advanced packaging) revenue is tracking ~USD 200M AHEAD of the USD 3.5B 2026 guidance and management is aiming to DOUBLE LEAP revenue in 2027. Full-process CoWoS-like packaging is on track for ~USD 300M in 2026 with substantial growth in 2027 and is expected to be margin-accretive. ASE's fully automated PANEL line (310mm x 310mm) enters production in Q1 2027, complementary to foundry CoWoS and serving the same customer set at similar reticle size and pitch. Capacity — not demand — is the constraint: blended utilization 80-85% but effectively full, with growth gated by equipment installation and building construction (13 greenfield plus 8 brownfield projects underway). FY2026 capex raised USD 2B to ~USD 10.5B, ~70% of equipment capex going to leading edge.
LEAP ~USD 3.7B 2026, DOUBLING in 2027; full-process ~USD 300M; panel 310x310mm production Q1 2027

GENERAL-MARKET OSAT OUTLOOK MORE THAN DOUBLED: the non-LEAP/general segment is now expected to grow ~30% YoY in 2026 versus the previous 13% guidance, on strong demand in INDUSTRIAL, POWER, CONNECTIVITY and STORAGE devices. Non-LEAP capacity is tight — legacy WIRE BOND and traditional advanced packaging were both tight in Q2, and assembly (led by legacy wire bond) is now growing at least as fast as test, reversing the expectation that wafer-sort-led test would outpace assembly. Blended utilization 80-85% but effectively full outside newly installed lines; ASE must add capacity for mainstream advanced packaging and test alongside LEAP. Record ATM revenue NTD 126.1B (+36% YoY) with ATM gross margin 27.3%.
general segment now +30% YoY (was 13%); wire bond tight; assembly matching test growth

CAPACITY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT: blended utilization 80-85%, but 'outside of equipment lines being placed into service, capacities were generally very close to being full' — non-LEAP wire bond and traditional advanced packaging were tight, and wafer sort and final test were running near full. 'Our capability for near-term incremental growth is being gated by our abilities to install capital equipment and build out our buildings and facilities.' Dr. Wu frames HARDWARE INFRASTRUCTURE as the new bottleneck ('we have not experienced this for the last 40 years') and argues packaging is moving up the system-architecture value chain. On the Q3 guide: '12%-13% growth... means we have to add 12%-13% capacity'; all customers are asking for more devices in Q3 and Q4.
utilization 80-85% but effectively full; growth gated by equipment install + building construction

Technology roadmap. PANEL: ASE's fully automated panel line starts PRODUCTION IN Q1 2027 in a 310mm x 310mm form factor — described as COMPLEMENTARY to foundry CoWoS, serving the SAME CUSTOMER SET with identical reticle size and pitch/line-width coverage; adoption depends on capacity, performance and speed of execution. GLASS SUBSTRATE: NOT in production and not within the next 12 months; R&D is evaluating feasibility and economics with substrate suppliers, the foundry and customers. FULL-PROCESS (CoWoS-like): on track for ~USD 300M of revenue in 2026 with aggressive capacity expansion and substantial growth in 2027; margin not yet fully reflected but expected to be margin-accretive. CPO: launching toward the END OF 2026 in initially small volume, yielding benchmark data on bandwidth, system performance and thermal dissipation; more detail promised in two quarters. Bigger reticle sizes drive panel/more-complex CoWoS first, then POWER DELIVERY becomes the next constraint over the following two to three years.
panel 310x310mm production Q1 2027; glass substrate not within 12 months; full-process ~USD 300M 2026; CPO launches late 2026

Service-mix and competitive positioning. ASSEMBLY IS NOW KEEPING PACE WITH TEST: entering the year management expected test (led by rapid wafer-sort expansion) to outgrow assembly, but assembly has grown even more strongly than expected — 'especially as it relates to LEGACY WIRE BOND services' — so both are now expected to grow at similar rates in 2026 and in the 2027 LEAP mix. Computing applications keep rising as a share of ATM revenue, a trend management sees continuing into 2027 and 2028. On EMIB as a CoWoS alternative, Dr. Wu is deliberately agnostic: as a PURE-PLAY OSAT with 'no conflict with foundry, no conflict with substrate provider', 'if the EMIB substrate becomes the right alternative, we'll just buy EMIB substrate and we do the assembly' — not a zero-sum threat. U.S. footprint: test development and services in California with factories in Fremont and San Jose, extending to a third and fourth site; but manufacturing PROCESS development stays in Taiwan until scale and efficiency are proven, then migrates.
assembly now matching test growth (legacy wire bond strong); EMIB treated as pure-play-neutral

HBM INSPECTION RAMPING ACROSS GENERATIONS: during Q2 Cohu shipped additional FINAL INSPECTION SYSTEMS FOR HBM3, HBM4 AND HBM4E devices to a US-BASED IDM (not named), with a strong forecast into the second half of 2026, and says it continues to invest to stay ahead of customer road maps INTO HBM5 AND BEYOND — calling HBM 'the memory backbone of AI training and inference infrastructure'. Cohu also QUALIFIED ITS NEON PLATFORM AT A TAIWAN-BASED OSAT (not named), establishing a foothold in high-volume outsourced assembly from which it intends to pursue further advanced-package and AI-adjacent inspection opportunities. New capability released in the quarter: a vision inspection sensor with SHORTWAVE INFRARED that detects INNER CRACKS in complex silicon devices — described as a step-change in outgoing quality for advanced packages.
HBM3/HBM4/HBM4E final-inspection shipments to a US IDM; roadmap to HBM5; Neon qualified at a Taiwan OSAT

TCB: in July 2026 the group received new bulk orders for more than 50 C2S TCB tools from OSAT customers (majority delivering in Q1 2027, some in the second half of 2026); a C2W bulk order secured in Q2 from a leading global IDM for advanced CPUs supporting client computing and AI inferencing; ultra-fine-pitch TCB tools delivered to the leading advanced logic customer; chip-to-wafer demand expected more meaningful in 2027 as next-generation GPUs may move to chiplet architectures. TCB TAM expected to expand beyond $1.6 billion by 2028 on data center CPU demand, larger packaging requirements and panel-level packaging.
more than 50 C2S TCB tools ordered in July 2026; TCB TAM beyond $1.6 billion by 2028

HBM: continued repeat orders from HBM manufacturers; installed tools at one customer now deployed to HBM4 in high volume manufacturing, plus low volume manufacturing with multiple memory makers for HBM4; entered an exclusive joint evaluation program with a key memory player for HBM5 advanced memory packaging. Data center design and power efficiency: Sweetwater 1 is becoming the reference design for Sweetwater 2, Kiowa, Bundey and later projects, with common layouts and equipment plus more modularisation and prefab, explicitly built for successive GPU generations and evolving cooling INCLUDING 800-VOLT DC, all developed in collaboration with NVIDIA - a direct answer to the bear case that AI data centers get rebuilt in ten years. IREN also expects to extract more from sites it already owns: existing sites have SPARE POWER BEYOND CURRENT DEPLOYMENT PLANS that can support more GPUs and revenue WITHOUT NEW GRID CAPACITY, the scarcest input in the industry, starting with new liquid-cooled installs at Mackenzie, Canal Flats and Prince George in 2027. Tools such as NVIDIA MaxLPS, which smooths GPU power draw, and the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture, which runs chips at higher temperatures without giving up performance, let IREN direct more of each megawatt to IT load. Headline PUE has been deliberately conservative at 200 megawatts of IT load for 300 megawatts of gross capacity, and IREN uses a highly efficient CLOSED-LOOP liquid cooling system with minimal ongoing water usage.

IREN said it welcomes the additional transparency and is positioned well with two very large already-energised Texas sites, and expects a tighter interconnection process to favour real and well-capitalised projects. Co-CEO Daniel Roberts framed the macro backdrop with the observation that across eight models tracked by OpenRouter, weekly token usage across large language models increased NEARLY 17x IN 8 MONTHS, which is very difficult to serve with infrastructure on three-year lead times.

POWER franchise detail: customers are pushing for greater than 98% conversion efficiency, multi-kilowatt delivery with peak power up to 2x rated load, plus protection, telemetry and fault recording. Significant design uptick for ADI protection and 800V-to-intermediate conversion technology delivering 20 kW at industry-leading power density exceeding 2.5 kW per cubic inch, as the industry transitions to 800V DC power distribution. At the intermediate-to-core conversion layer - called ONE OF THE FASTEST AND LARGEST GROWING ANALOG OPPORTUNITIES IN THE AI ERA - ADI combines advanced power conversion, intelligent system control and real-time telemetry for next-generation processors operating at 6,000 A and sub-1V. Framing on efficiency: a 97% converter loses roughly 50% more energy as heat than a 98% one, compounding into cooling infrastructure and opex.

GRID-TO-CHIP strategy: data center capacity is now measured in GIGAWATTS rather than FLOPS/TOPS and POWER AVAILABILITY HAS BECOME THE PRIMARY CONSTRAINT TO FURTHER AI PROGRESS. ADI supplies grid monitoring (real-time voltage, current, power quality, system health) to utilities, energy operators and infrastructure providers, plus battery management for energy storage - one of the grid's fastest-growing sectors. To accelerate time-to-power, hyperscalers are increasingly exploring DEDICATED MICROGRIDS, opening additional growth avenues that augment ADI's $500M+ energy business (inflected in 2025, accelerating in 2026). ADI now spans the entire electricity value chain: generation, transmission, storage, distribution, rack power and ultimately processor power delivery - 'essentially the vascular system of the data center.'

2030 SAM RESET: ADI's current assessment is that its 2030 data center AND energy SAM has MORE THAN DOUBLED versus what it envisioned just one year ago - driven not simply by higher AI infrastructure CapEx but by new markets and architectures requiring ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE MORE ANALOG CONTENT delivered via higher-value solutions. THREE-TIER DEAL MODEL made explicit. (1) MID-TERM core AI cloud contracts of one to three years — four landmark deals closed in Q2 with REFLECTION, COHERE, an unnamed scale U.S. Neolab and a large U.S.-based quant trading firm, averaging MORE THAN $1B EACH at a yield of $20-25M PER MEGAWATT, upfront payments covering 50-60% of associated capex and payback under two years. (2) SHORT-DURATION capacity of up to six months for time-boxed needs (large training runs before a model release, RL post-training sprints) on dedicated GB300 clusters, being negotiated at $40-50M PER MEGAWATT 'and sometimes above' — roughly double the mid-term yield; one such deal signed recently. (3) LONG-TERM contracts with investment-grade customers, used primarily to finance the build-out. Management states it COULD SELL ITS ENTIRE 2027 CAPACITY TODAY on mid-term terms but is deliberately choosing NOT TO, retaining capacity for higher-value short-term demand; it has also tactically shortened how far in advance it sells, selling closer to deployment to improve realized pricing.
mid-term $20-25M/MW vs short-term $40-50M/MW; could sell out 2027 today but choosing not to

FIRST CAPACITY AUCTION as a price-discovery mechanism: it cleared at the highest price Nebius has ever seen for the BLACKWELL generation — 15% ABOVE THE HIGHEST PRICE IT HAD EVER CHARGED and 20% ABOVE its Blackwell pipeline pricing. Management framed it as letting the market set price directly in an environment where 'competitor pricing, analyst opinions, and even prediction markets are all over the place' and 'we have several buyers for every GPU'; the winning bidder plans to participate in future rounds. Both the auction and the short-term scale-training deals remain take-or-pay, use only a small portion of total capacity, and have faster close-to-deployment cycles. On competitive entry (xAI selling compute at premium prices), CEO Arkady Volozh said new entrants 'validate the market' — the AI cloud market is growing tens of gigawatts per year while Nebius plans roughly 1 GW per year, so hyperscalers 'cannot build all of it'.
first auction cleared 15% above highest price ever charged, 20% above Blackwell pipeline

Deployment timing, not demand, is the constraint: Q4 revenue of $11.1B landed near the low end of guidance because large datacenter and Neocloud customers were not ready on power, cooling and networking - a timing story with the revenue expected in subsequent quarters, and OEM/large-DC revenue fell 26% QoQ to $5.5B while enterprise/channel doubled. DCBBS is pitched as the answer to the readiness problem - a one-stop shop (power, DLC, CDU, chill door, water tower, 1.6T switching, management software, lifecycle service) that lets customers build AI datacenters in quarters rather than years and improves time-to-deployment (TTD) and time-to-online (TTO).

DCBBS is the response: a turnkey stack of DLC solutions, CDU, chill door, water tower, power shelves/battery backup, 1.6T high-speed switching and networking, Supermicro Data Center Management software (SCM, SuperCloud Composer, SVM, SOM Orchestration Manager) and full lifecycle services, plus a new PROACTIVE SERVICE model going online early next quarter where management software and field teams auto-alert and pre-stage repairs to stop compute capacity loss. Liquid cooling penetration keeps rising - GPU and CPU platforms alike (Vera, Rubin) are liquid-cooling-ready and management expects liquid cooling to dominate the datacenter business soon.

Future power projects 'more likely than not' take place in the Ohio campus.

Customer demand described as 'unconstrained': on the power side 'we've already had the Meta payment, we've had the Equinix payment' and those discussions are the most advanced; every execution milestone 'creates more credibility and it does help those conversations'. Data-center heat-and-power collaboration with Vertiv (heat-driven cooling) announced last year.

Fuel supply — the key deployment constraint — is being diversified: Centrus letter of intent for HALEU covering initial core and reload needs for up to five Aurora powerhouses for multiple years with deliveries expected to begin in 2029 (possible Oklo/customer prepayments to fund the Ohio build-out); DOE selected Oklo for advanced negotiations on surplus plutonium (about 20 tons in the tranche) that as blended bridge fuel 'supports up to potentially 2 gigawatts'; Aurora Fuel Fabrication Facility (A3F) equipment now in production for 2027 installation; Advanced Fuel Center recycling facility in Tennessee advancing NRC license readiness.
Centrus HALEU for up to five Aurora powerhouses from 2029; plutonium bridge fuel up to ~2 GW

THE STRANDED-CAPACITY THESIS, restated as the core commercial argument: the grid has unused generation and wires capacity in OVER 99% OF THE HOURS of the year - 'we have a peak capacity concern, not an energy concern' - so the fastest and cheapest path to powering AI is harvesting that latent capacity and managing the handful of peak hours with batteries, demand response, peaking resources and customer backup generation. Management argues existing and new supply are not bifurcated: even a customer that self-manages peaks via Connect and Manage 'will still need to buy energy for all of the other hours', which is where the existing fixed-price, carbon-free nuclear fleet becomes the multi-decade product customers want. Customer sophistication about the grid is now 'as good as the energy companies themselves' - not true two years ago. Management expects the data economy to invest 'upwards of $1 trillion in infrastructure ANNUALLY' and expects PJM deal flow to 'kick off with a bit of a bang' once rules are final
grid unused >99% of hours; data economy capex 'upwards of $1T annually'

Houston 15 GWh/yr, full production fiscal Q1 2027; China site reworked, full production in Q4; ~$400M of FY26 revenue pushed to FY27

mid-teens levered return threshold; Helix absorbs powered-land/shell capital

ERCOT QUEUE REALITY CHECK: Vistra's May-2024 forecast of 115-120 GW of ERCOT load in 2030 is UNCHANGED despite the queue growing to what has at times been expressed as OVER 400 GW — Vistra thinks the real data-center number is 12-15 GW by 2030, i.e. the queue overstates demand by MORE THAN 20x. ERCOT 2030 load 115-120 GW (unchanged); queue >400 GW vs real DC 12-15 GW = >20x overstated

ERCOT YTD $30/MWh vs ~$90 new build; equipment costs 2-3x; PJM RPB cap $555/MW-day

Battery returns since the large post-August-2023 ECRS payments have been about ONE FIFTH of investor expectations and battery queues are slowing. Vistra reads current ERCOT softness as recency bias plus lumpy load timing; the load it expects to hook up was always a 2027-2028 event.
Jul 22: ~25 GWh needed of ~31 GWh available, cleared $57 vs potential $400-500; battery returns ~1/5 of expectations

>97% commercial availability; 3 nuclear refuels + 92 planned outages

Data center power is GF's third named growth pillar alongside silicon photonics and SiGe. In July GF closed a strategic acquihire of the custom power team from Photon Technologies in Europe, bringing an experienced design team focused on INTEGRATED VOLTAGE REGULATORS (IVRs). Combined with GF's BCD, GaN and integrated-inductor capabilities, the goal is a new power architecture that brings power conversion closer to the processor to meet the efficiency, power density, bandwidth, high-current and transient-response requirements of next-generation XPUs. CEO Tim Breen framed it directly: 'IVR is to power what CPO is to photonics' - moving from traditional industrial/automotive-style power modules to a much more wafer-level integrated solution delivering power closer to the chip. The Photon team is already engaged with a number of existing GF customers, and early feedback from fabless companies, IDMs and hyperscalers has been very positive.

GF closed a first-of-a-kind design win for SMART POWER STAGE GATE DRIVERS on its BCD platform for data center power applications, which management called one notable step into a rapidly evolving market. The quarter also brought a significant automotive power design win for 5-volt and 10-volt power management integrated circuits on BCD, and a first-ever PMIC design win with long-standing customer MediaTek on the same platform - evidence that the BCD power platform is expanding across data center, automotive and mobile.
First-of-a-kind smart power stage gate driver design win on BCD; automotive 5V/10V PMIC win; first-ever MediaTek PMIC win

Arista rejects the ~5 proprietary CPO implementations circulating and is committing to ONE OPEN CPO — socketed optical engines, pigtail fibers, fully pre-tested modules, a truly open multi-vendor interface (often called NPO) — with trials/examples NEXT YEAR; 'the MAJORITY of the world will still remain PLUGGABLE OPTICS AND COPPER; there will be SOME co-packaged optics in 2028 and 2029.' large-load contracts up to 20 years; take-or-pay minimums up to 80-90% of contracted demand; Virginia tariff threshold 150 MW aggregated / 100 MW individual

→ Google: CEO Bill Fehrman on Indiana: the planned base rate reductions 'are made possible by the ability to attract large load customers like Google and Microsoft, then shifting a significant amount of those fixed costs away from residential customers' — naming Google as a large-load customer of Indiana Michigan Power.

→ Microsoft: CEO Bill Fehrman on Indiana: the planned base rate reductions 'are made possible by the ability to attract large load customers like Google and Microsoft, then shifting a significant amount of those fixed costs away from residential customers' — naming Microsoft as a large-load customer of Indiana Michigan Power.

H2 is expected to be better than H1, with Q3 seasonally the strongest quarter; margins are seen holding around current levels - management cautions against expecting further margin expansion even as large CSP customers ramp, and says needed price increases for higher raw-material costs will be passed on with a timing lag. AI-related products will exceed 25% of group revenue this year (versus the roughly 20% target given earlier); the group grew 31% last year and this year should be higher. Hyperscaler capex keeps rising - the majors indicated this year's capex goes higher still and 2027 should increase again - so the AI data-center build-out is not expected to stop near term, though construction delays, key-component issues and US public sentiment (strong local opposition to data centers; New York state paused fifty-mega-scale projects by executive order) are watch items. Mobility (EV) stays weak this year with contained losses, while the BA unit returns to normal shipments in H2 after memory-sourcing design changes.
AI-related products above 25% of revenue this year (prior target about 20%); group revenue +31% last year with higher growth expected this year

HVDC ramp: plus/minus 400V and 800V systems start mass production in Q3 2026, but Q4 shipments and full-year volume stay limited - larger volume comes next year. The plus/minus 400V architecture is being pushed more aggressively and ships more this year; 800V is driven mainly by NVIDIA and depends on when data-center operators adopt that power architecture - NVIDIA's Blackwell shipments are still much larger than Rubin, and part of the Rubin lineup can still run on low voltage. On the 110kW power shelf and other new product cycles Delta believes its market share remains high because it engages customers earliest, and the fast generational churn of AI power architecture favors its engineering resources; it declined to quantify share for the Rubin-linked 110kW PSU but asserts market leadership. A solid-state transformer (an energy gateway, not a one-for-one transformer replacement) has its first trial customers in smaller data centers, and a first small fuel-cell line starts by year-end with the first volume line planned next year, with units at Taipower and another test site performing well.
HVDC plus/minus 400V and 800V mass production from Q3, limited volume this year, ramp next year; 110kW power shelf share seen high

Liquid cooling keeps scaling: liquid-cooling products were about 10% of group revenue last year and will exceed 12% this year (an analyst cited about US$1.6 billion of Liquid-to-Air contribution last year). Management expects Liquid-to-Air to persist considerably longer than the market's assumption that Liquid-to-Liquid fully takes over around 2028.
liquid cooling about 10% of revenue last year, above 12% this year; Liquid-to-Air about US$1.6B contribution last year

Capacity is being pre-built for multi-year AI and energy demand: Thailand plant 1 is being rebuilt with several times its old capacity and three more Thai plants finish this year and next; China, Taiwan and the US are all expanding, a US building was bought for R&D, and one more overseas operations site is under negotiation. H1 capex was NT$275 hundred million and H2 will exceed NT$400 hundred million - roughly NT$700 hundred million for the year versus NT$466 hundred million last year; if next year's growth stays high, capex stays at that level or higher. Large customers are already booking next year's volumes and the requested amounts are big; beyond AI, the next demand leg is energy infrastructure/microgrid (grid, self-generation, energy storage), where single projects run to several hundred million dollars. From April this year all AI-related equipment is depreciated over 3 years (previously up to 5) as a conservative policy.
H1 capex NT$275 hundred million, H2 above NT$400 hundred million, about NT$700 hundred million full year vs NT$466 hundred million last year

Component supply is tight across the board: lead times are stretching and MOSFETs in particular are short, though Delta's purchasing scale and supplier relationships keep demand largely fulfilled. Memory was the hardest hit - one business unit could not secure memory volumes at workable prices, so it switched designs to second sources and expects H2 shipments to normalize and catch up the backlog without a loss. Management does not expect power semiconductors to repeat memory's shortage dynamics - the two situations differ a lot - but notes power-semi supply is cyclical because capacity investment takes long. On wide-bandgap devices (silicon carbide, gallium nitride) Delta works early and closely with the most important suppliers, keeps talking with them continuously and gets early access to new products, but will not disclose any agreements; it is also broadening its supply chain, including Taiwanese supplier options. Supplier price increases will be negotiated and passed to customers where the business model allows, with a timing lag.

EMCOR's 10-Q splits remaining performance obligations at June 30, 2026 by segment: U.S. electrical construction and facilities services $6,271,919 thousand (36%) and U.S. mechanical construction and facilities services $9,366,637 thousand (55%), versus $11.91 billion total RPO at June 30, 2025; $13,023,427 thousand of total RPO is expected to be recognized within one year. electrical construction RPO $6,271,919 thousand (36%); mechanical construction RPO $9,366,637 thousand (55%) at June 30, 2026; RPO $11.91 billion at June 30, 2025; +$3.89 billion since December 31, 2025

DATA CENTERS ARE NOW EMCOR'S PRINCIPAL GROWTH ENGINE. Record quarterly revenue $5.15B (+19.8%, +19.6% organic). ELECTRICAL CONSTRUCTION $1.66B (+24%) at a 13.9% operating margin, where 'the majority of its growth in the quarter resulted from greater DATA CENTER PROJECTS within the network and communications market sector, where REVENUES INCREASED BY 45%'. MECHANICAL CONSTRUCTION $2.3B (+31%) at ~12.5% margin, where network-and-communications revenue MORE THAN DOUBLED year over year — driven explicitly by 'INCREASED COOLING REQUIREMENTS FOR DATA CENTERS' plus expansion into new and adjacent geographies. Combined construction revenue $3.96B (+28%), a quarterly record for both segments. Building Services $837.7M (+5.6%) with operating income +26.6%; Industrial Services +26%.
Record revenue $5.15B (+19.8%); electrical DC revenue +45%, mechanical network/comms MORE THAN DOUBLED

Exelon's Q2 2026 earnings presentation (Exhibit 99.2), slide 'Exelon's Projected Data Center Growth', splits projected data center growth into ~11 GW of High Probability Load (ComEd ~9 GW, MidAtlantic ~2 GW), described on the slide as 'Advanced phases of design or backed by FERC-approved TSAs (~40% with TSAs, backed by ~$1B in collateral)', and a ~25 GW Future Pipeline (ComEd ~17 GW, MidAtlantic ~8 GW) 'within current or future cluster studies (2026 and 2027 conclusion)'. The deck lists '$1B+ associated with committed high-density load projects' as the New Business category of its identified transmission opportunity, says its network serves 4 major cities including a top 5 data center market and a top 3 emerging data center market, and lists 'ComEd Announces New TSAs of 6.5+ GW' dated January 6, 2026.

high probability load ~11 GW (ComEd ~9 GW, MidAtlantic ~2 GW); future pipeline ~25 GW (ComEd ~17 GW, MidAtlantic ~8 GW); $1B+ transmission for committed high-density load projects; ComEd new TSAs 6.5+ GW

A RARE DOWNWARD REVISION TO A DATA-CENTER PIPELINE — AND WHY IT MATTERS: Exelon's data-center growth pipeline now shows a combined 36 GIGAWATTS, DOWN ROUGHLY 11 GW FROM THE 43 GW previously cited. CFO Jeanne Jones attributes the cut not to demand weakness but to Exelon's own screening discipline: it developed TRANSMISSION SECURITY AGREEMENTS (TSAs) that 'never existed in our regions', and its cluster process now requires a customer to sign a TSA and, importantly, 'PUT UP COLLATERAL BEHIND THAT'. The result: 'what this update reflects is we have now WEEDED OUT SPECULATIVE PROJECTS, and it gives us proactive insight into what is real.' Exelon says it has deliberately kept capex increases consistent with historical levels and only committed capital that was 'certain and durable', alongside its stance on CO-LOCATION and fair cost allocation to shield existing customers from infrastructure costs. This is a useful reality-check datapoint on how much of the headline AI interconnection queue is firm versus speculative.
Data-centre pipeline cut 43 GW -> 36 GW after TSA + COLLATERAL requirements weeded out speculative projects

→ American Electric Power: AEP CEO Bill Fehrman names its turbine suppliers: 'using our size and scale and our relationships with namely GE Vernova and Mitsubishi to get this equipment locked up.' AEP secured an additional three gigawatts of turbines in the quarter, taking total secured turbine capacity to approximately 13 gigawatts for deployment through 2031, and has clear line of sight through framework agreements to up to 10 gigawatts of incremental turbine capacity through 2035. The vendor split between GE Vernova and Mitsubishi was not disclosed.

units: Approximately 13 GW of turbine capacity secured for deployment through 2031 (three gigawatts added this quarter); option on up to 10 GW of incremental capacity through 2035 — vendor split not disclosed

First quarter reported under the new three-segment structure (Data Centers, Commercial HVAC, Performance Technologies). Data Center segment revenue increased 90% year-over-year — Americas sales grew 112% and EMEA sales increased 18%, 'mainly from growth with strategic hyperscale and colocation customers' — but was down sequentially from Q4 because component shortages limited production volume. Data Center adjusted EBITDA grew 27%, giving a 14.8% adjusted EBITDA margin (down year-over-year). Total company sales rose 28%; adjusted EPS was $1.53, 44% higher than the prior year; adjusted EBITDA grew 5% (a $5.1 million increase) with margin down 270 basis points to 12.2% and gross margin down 340 basis points to 20.8%.
DC revenue +90% YoY (Americas +112%, EMEA +18%); DC adj EBITDA +27%, margin 14.8%; total sales +28%, adj EPS $1.53 (+44%)

Component shortages were the quarter's defining constraint. Critical suppliers 'essentially shut a lot of us down with a hard stop' and the shortages hit faster and lasted longer than anticipated; Modine had previously flagged four suppliers as potential vulnerabilities in its risk-management process. Because plants were already being staffed and prepared for significantly higher volume, the part shortages caused temporary downtime and lower-than-planned capacity utilisation across the expansion sites: excess labour plus unfavourable overhead absorption on the lower volumes had a 450-550 basis point impact on Data Center margin in the quarter, on top of a 150 basis point year-over-year warranty variance from a large prior-year settlement. Modine repositioned available parts to its highest-producing, most efficient lines and idled others, and rationed supply so that its largest key accounts got priority over smaller customers. By the third month of the quarter (June) Data Center margin was 'right back where we'd expect it to be,' and management said it has now secured the supply chain needed to meet demand for the rest of the year.
450-550 bps Data Center margin impact from excess labour/overhead absorption; 150 bps warranty variance; four suppliers flagged as vulnerable; June margin back to normal

Structural response to the shortage: Modine is actively negotiating long-term agreements with its critical component suppliers covering FY 2028 and FY 2029 and expects them in place soon, its existing suppliers are expanding capacity to meet market demand, and in one instance Modine is considering vertical integration. Management noted it has doubled supply-chain spend year after year as the business has grown, and has brought in senior operations talent at plant level to negotiate these long-term contracts and dynamically rebalance launch schedules against available component capacity.
supplier LTAs targeted for FY2028 and FY2029; vertical integration under consideration in one case

Third consecutive quarter of record order intake, driving another significant increase in backlog (analysts on the call referred to backlog more than doubling; management did not quantify it). The drivers were the three largest data-center customers — a couple of hyperscalers plus one large neocloud provider — all raising their forecasts as their data-center build-outs grow; none were named on the call. Order growth is concentrated in air handling units and chillers. On coverage, Modine typically starts a fiscal year with roughly 70%-80% of revenue in firm orders, with firm POs about six months out (two quarters), softer visibility in Q3 and no firm POs yet in Q4 — those Q4 POs, including against the hyperscaler capacity LTA, arrive as the year rolls forward.
third straight record order quarter; roughly 70%-80% of fiscal-year revenue in firm orders at year start; firm POs about six months out

The hyperscaler chiller capacity LTA has begun converting into orders: Modine has already taken a couple of orders against it and expected more 'as early as next week,' in line with its Q4 order-intake expectation, on a typical four-to-six-month lead time from order to build. Management gave the roll-out cadence for the first time: 20%-25% of the agreement in 2027 and 35%-40% in each of 2028 and 2029. The LTA absorbs about half of Modine's chiller capacity, a share expected to fall over time as product manufacturing gets more efficient and the three-megawatt chiller launches. Other customers are in discussions for their own agreements, but sized at 12-18 months rather than the three-year scale of the first hyperscaler deal.
LTA cadence 20%-25% in 2027 and 35%-40% in each of 2028 and 2029; ~half of chiller capacity; follow-on agreements sized at 12-18 months

Fiscal 2027 outlook unchanged: total company sales to grow 20%-35%, Data Center segment sales 60%-80%, Commercial HVAC 5%-10%, Performance Technologies flat to up 5%. Adjusted EBITDA of $650 million-$680 million, a growth rate in excess of 40%, implying at least 100-200 basis points of margin improvement with all three segments improving; free cash flow of 4%-6% of sales. The Data Center segment specifically is expected to generate earnings growth in excess of 85% this year. Management also reaffirmed the 50%-70% Data Center organic growth framework previously laid out for fiscal 2028 ('we're confident in the numbers that we put out'), and noted Data Center revenue has compounded at more than 80% a year over the last three years.
FY2027: DC sales +60%-80%, total sales +20%-35%, adj EBITDA $650-680M (+40%+); DC segment earnings growth in excess of 85%; FY2028 DC +50%-70% reaffirmed

Margin recovery path quantified: Data Center revenue is expected to rise about $100 million sequentially in Q2, putting it back ahead of the Q4 FY2026 level and lifting the segment's adjusted EBITDA margin back to 19%-20% from 14.8% as fixed costs are re-absorbed. Management expects a further step-up in Q3 over Q2 and again in Q4, with the second half operating above the 20% EBITDA margin range for the first time in a while. Company-wide, Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin is expected to lift roughly 200-250 basis points sequentially.
Q2 Data Center revenue +~$100M sequentially, margin back to 19%-20%; second half above 20%; company margin +200-250 bps in Q2

Capacity ceiling stated: with the capex already deployed and the facilities and rooftops it has in place today, Modine believes the range is 'right around $4 billion' of revenue it can support over time. Going beyond that would require a different level of capex outlay, or a combination of an incremental facility, more efficiency on existing lines, and leveraging the supply chain to produce overflow capacity; design work is moving toward a more modular systems approach in the factory to add flexibility. The remaining chiller lines in Grenada, Jefferson City and the Dallas area are expected to be up and established at some level of efficiency by the end of the fiscal year. Coils production has been consolidated into Grenada and Juarez to allow the Grenada chiller lines to expand while preserving coil capacity for data-center customers; Heat Transfer Solutions sales improved 7%, or $11 million, on strong North America coil volume supporting data-center customers.
~$4 billion of revenue capacity on current capex and footprint; Grenada, Jefferson City and Dallas chiller lines running by end of fiscal 2027; coil sales +7% / $11M on data-center demand

Technology read-through on evolving cooling architectures: asked whether higher inlet fluid temperature specs for future GPU designs reduce chiller demand, management said demand is improving and increasing for Modine because of its free-cooling technology — a higher inlet temperature lets the unit run in free-cooling mode more of the time, driving further efficiency and reducing data-center power consumption, while the chiller and refrigerant cycle stay in place as the 'insurance policy' for temperatures above that band. Chillers support both facility cooling and incorporation into direct-to-chip liquid cooling systems — similar models and SKUs sit on the same data-center rooftop doing both — so Modine cannot split its order book between the two. The enhanced three-megawatt chiller is being introduced to customers and will raise output per line versus the 2 MW unit.
3 MW chiller launching (vs 2 MW today); higher GPU inlet temperatures increase free-cooling/chiller demand

A customer program delay pushed volume out of the quarter: the modular data-center product being co-designed with a specific hyperscaler is in roughly its third iteration of the design cycle, and updates to the prints and overall product specifications moved the build out of Q1. Management stressed this was a new product launch slipping, not chiller orders being cancelled or pushed out. A few shipments also slipped at the very end of the quarter. Modine's other new product launches were described as a commercial success, with the strategic customer focus on 'high-quality hyperscalers, neoclouds, and co-location customers.'

Modine's 10-Q: Data Centers segment operating income was $46.3 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026 versus $34.7 million a year earlier. Data Centers cost of sales rose $149.3 million, or 116 percent, on higher sales volume, approximately $16.0 million of higher material costs, expenses of the rapid U.S. manufacturing capacity expansion, and supplier capacity constraints for certain key components that temporarily disrupted production schedules; Modine is working with current partners and qualifying additional suppliers to secure supply. Data Centers capital expenditures were $30.9 million versus $7.1 million, driven by investments to increase production capacity.

Data Centers operating income $46.3 million vs $34.7 million; Data Centers cost of sales +$149.3 million (+116 percent), material costs +~$16.0 million; Data Centers capex $30.9 million vs $7.1 million

RECORD Q2 2026 revenue $981M (+22% QoQ, +48% YoY) with ALL end markets growing sequentially and ENTERPRISE DATA +45% SEQUENTIALLY on 'strong broad based ordering patterns'. Capacity goals extended SIGNIFICANTLY BEYOND $6 BILLION to support the transformation from chip supplier to full-solution provider. Began sampling high-voltage AC-to-DC for 800V data-center architectures (silicon-carbide based). Book-to-bill again well above 1 with more than a quarter of visibility. Board authorized an additional $500M buyback (total authorization now $1B).
Record $981M (+48% YoY); enterprise data +45% QoQ; capacity goal >$6B

Record Q2 2026 revenue $981M (+22% QoQ, +48% YoY); enterprise data +45% sequentially and COMMUNICATIONS ~+80% (from ~+50% prior quarter) on power for optical modules plus top-of-rack switches, TPUs and NIC cards. Capacity goals extended significantly BEYOND $6B as MPS shifts from chip supplier to full-solution provider. Sampling 800V AC-to-DC (silicon-carbide based) for data-center architectures; initial orders received for high-speed DDR5 memory products. Additional $500M buyback authorized (total $1B).
Record $981M (+48% YoY); enterprise data +45% QoQ; comms ~+80%; capacity >$6B

Two new content vectors moved forward. (1) MEMORY: received INITIAL ORDERS for high-speed DDR5 memory products (sampled at major customers last quarter), which MPS expects to GROW ITS SAM into next year. (2) 800V DATA CENTER: began SAMPLING high-voltage AC-to-DC products for 800-volt data-center architectures, expanding beyond current AI/server core power. MPS's 800V solution relies on ITS OWN SILICON CARBIDE devices, not GaN — though CEO Michael Hsing conceded he had been 'proven wrong' on GaN ('it is up to a point where we cannot ignore GaN'), noting MPS developed its own GaN last year and has a working device. Revenue timing for 800V is explicitly gated on when the data-center transition actually occurs. Also shipping 48V VERTICAL POWER MODULES to more than a couple of customers with new ones coming online, and >1,500 new automotive sockets shipped year-to-date across ADAS and other in-vehicle applications.
Initial DDR5 memory orders; 800V AC-DC sampling on MPS SiC; 48V vertical modules at multiple customers

Energy storage systems (ESS) for data centers: strong growth continues as expected on generative-AI demand (Panasonic Energy industrial/consumer AOP significantly increased on higher ESS sales for data centers). Supply capability being expanded rapidly: cell production lines in Japan being converted from automotive applications, cell mass production at the Kansas factory planned for fiscal 2029; module production - second Mexico plant starts mass production in Q2 of fiscal 2027, third plant in fiscal 2028, with localization of the broader supply chain including power supply manufacturers advancing. BBU: full-year aim of 1.7 times or JPY 550 billion maintained, based on demand information collected from hyperscalers. Product evolution: CBU solutions (combining in-house batteries and capacitors with Industry) start mass production in fiscal 2027; preparations for mass production of next-generation BBU built for HVDC to be completed within fiscal 2027.
BBU full-year aim 1.7x / JPY 550 billion; Mexico module plant 2 mass production Q2 FY2027, plant 3 FY2028; Kansas cells FY2029; next-gen HVDC BBU within FY2027

BBU content growth with next-generation accelerators: asked about NVIDIA Rubin production starting and per-rack battery cell capacity possibly rising from 80 W to 120 W, management said the Rubin percentage will not be so high yet but Panasonic's portion will increase including capacity, and as the BBU solution evolves the unit price would go up - required output changes and the total solution expands ('it's not replacing PBU, but it's PBU plus CPU'); non-GPU demand (TPU, ASIC, including CPU racks for inference) is also expanding and is part of the JPY 550 billion full-year picture.
Per-rack battery cell capacity discussion 80 W to 120 W with Rubin; unit price to rise as BBU solution evolves

RECORD BACKLOG OF $53 BILLION - and the big work is not in it yet. Duke Austin: 'The record backlog we reported reflects the demand in front of us, but we're still in the early stages. The larger programs across the utility generation and technology load center markets are ahead of us, and we expect them to stack in the years to come.' The 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV transmission are still in engineering ('We're not in backlog on any of the bigger work yet'), and about 95% of the generation work is not in backlog either. He expects record backlog again in the third quarter and probably the fourth. Book-to-burn will be lumpy: 1:1 to 1:2 in ordinary quarters, 1:5 to 1:6 in quarters when big chunks of projects land (the 765 kV work brought in last quarter was that kind of boost) - 'lower lows and higher highs all the way through'. A large share of the technology work never touches backlog at all: MEP crews can 'book and bill $300 million on a site in a quarter' against an MSA and 'you never see it show up in backlog'. CFO Jayshree Desai on data-center backlog discipline: only items with limited notices to proceed go in, 'we don't put the rest in until the project is a confirmed go.'
Record total backlog $53B; ~95% of generation work not yet in backlog; up to $300M booked-and-burned on a single technology site per quarter, outside backlog

Craft labour is NOT the binding constraint today - Duke Austin: 'We're nowhere near capacity.' More than 85,000 employees; roughly 15,500 people added over the past year, well over 7,000 of them organic with a significant portion in Q2; Quanta spends about $250 million a year on training. It takes about four years to make a craftsman and a journeyman, and he sees no oversupply of craft-skilled labour in the near future. Labour is fungible across segments - electricians and underground crews move between data-center work, industrial and gas compression work and T&D - which is where the acquisition synergies show up. Customers are securing craft as far out as their five- to seven-year capital plans, with 'decade-plus type arrangements out there'. Margin follows that utilisation: the electric segment can operate at 10% to 12% on the utility side, with 12% the utmost 'when you stack in large transmission and all aspects at once', and Duke sees room for further margin improvement in the second half.
85,000+ employees, +15,500 over the year (>7,000 organic); ~$250M/yr training; 'nowhere near capacity'; electric segment margin range 10%-12% on the utility side

The stacking has not started. Duke Austin: the 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV projects and the generation work are 'just starting - a lot of it's in engineering'; they start hitting backlog in the later half of this year, crews go to the field around the second half of 2027, and the compounding effect then stacks out 'throughout what I would consider the decade' and 'well past 2030'. He compares it to 2012-2015, when a batch of big projects compounded, and says the base business is doing upper-single-digit to double-digit growth before any of that lands. The nearest concrete catalyst named on the call is the NiSource generation award: 'I do believe a significant amount of that will go into backlog in the third quarter.'

765 kV / 345 kV / 500 kV plus generation work moves into backlog in the later half of 2026, into the field in the second half of 2027, stacking well past 2030; NiSource generation award expected to enter backlog in the third quarter

VERTICAL INTEGRATION INTO CRITICAL-PATH EQUIPMENT. Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' The rule he states: 'Anywhere there's a critical path that we think we can invest capital to move it forward, that's what you've seen us do... we're taking advantage of areas where there's underinvestment', and those vertical supply-chain investments are 'showing up in synergies'. He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Done collaboratively with the client it takes total installed cost down significantly and de-risks logistics; the Phalcon acquisition puts that capacity in the Northeast, close to where the work is.
HICO high-voltage breaker JV plus owned transformer and utility-pole manufacturing; fabrication footprint ~seven million sq ft, +0.5 million sq ft from the recent acquisitions

Technology is now 15% to 20% of Quanta's business - 'a spectrum from chips to everything, not just data centers' - grown to that share over the last two years off the Cupertino Electric platform, and Duke Austin frames it as a second TAM 'every bit as big as our utility TAM'. Quanta sells direct to the hyperscalers and to the larger technology customers, and can self-perform 'call it 80% of what a data center build is, maybe 90%', taking balance-of-plant scope and full-scale data-center opportunities on more and more sites; it is also picking up work at semiconductor plants, at manufacturing and medical facilities, and at Tesla. The pitch is speed and certainty: 'Technology is trying to move as fast as possible. Utilities are working to protect the ratepayer, and Quanta sits in the middle of that nexus.' On state-level data-center moratoriums (New York): immaterial - 'nothing really gets built there' - and these are eight- to ten-year developments, not one-year builds, with multiyear projects extending well beyond 2030.
Technology = 15% to 20% of the business; Quanta can self-perform 80% to 90% of a data-center build

WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.
no specific figure (engine orders placed today carry a five- to six-year lead time; substation interconnection queue is the constraint)

HOW THE AI-LOAD CONTRACTS ARE CREDIT-PROTECTED - ABOUT $21 BILLION OF COLLATERAL BEHIND 17 GW. The large-load contracting framework has four pillars: long-term contracts (the OpenAI contract is 25 years), minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, default/termination provisions, and default payments tied to collateral. Poroch said forms of collateral include parent guarantees, lines of credit and surety bonds depending on counterparty credit quality, with the aim of a collateral portfolio equivalent to about A- or better. He initially cited '$20.8 billion of collateral... in the aggregate on full ramp' and then clarified that this refers to the entire portfolio: 'the whole portfolio of the 17 GW, we got about $21 billion of collateral.' Minimum bills effectively decouple revenue from actual customer ramp rates, which Womack said often differ from what was predicted at project approval.
About $21 billion of collateral in aggregate at full ramp across the 17 GW contracted portfolio; minimum bills cover 100% of incremental cost to serve

FIRST FLEXIBLE-DEMAND DATA CENTER: 1 GW OF DEMAND RESPONSE AT THE OPENAI SITE. The Savannah site features 1 GW of flexible demand response, and Womack confirmed this is the first time Southern has done that for a data center. Poroch said demand-response flexibility 'does enter into all those conversations' and is possible because the three electric jurisdictions are not limited to a tariff and can negotiate bilateral contracts that price hyperscaler flexibility. Womack said technical requirements - how a hyperscaler's operations affect the system and the grid, and whether it can be more than 'just a taker' - are raised very early in every hyperscaler conversation, and that peak shaving from this resource benefits the whole system.
1 GW of flexible demand response at the OpenAI Savannah site - Southern's first for a data center
