Component shortages were the quarter's defining constraint. Critical suppliers 'essentially shut a lot of us down with a hard stop' and the shortages hit faster and lasted longer than anticipated; Modine had previously flagged four suppliers as potential vulnerabilities in its risk-management process. Because plants were already being staffed and prepared for significantly higher volume, the part shortages caused temporary downtime and lower-than-planned capacity utilisation across the expansion sites: excess labour plus unfavourable overhead absorption on the lower volumes had a 450-550 basis point impact on Data Center margin in the quarter, on top of a 150 basis point year-over-year warranty variance from a large prior-year settlement. Modine repositioned available parts to its highest-producing, most efficient lines and idled others, and rationed supply so that its largest key accounts got priority over smaller customers. By the third month of the quarter (June) Data Center margin was 'right back where we'd expect it to be,' and management said it has now secured the supply chain needed to meet demand for the rest of the year.
450-550 bps Data Center margin impact from excess labour/overhead absorption; 150 bps warranty variance; four suppliers flagged as vulnerable; June margin back to normal

Structural response to the shortage: Modine is actively negotiating long-term agreements with its critical component suppliers covering FY 2028 and FY 2029 and expects them in place soon, its existing suppliers are expanding capacity to meet market demand, and in one instance Modine is considering vertical integration. Management noted it has doubled supply-chain spend year after year as the business has grown, and has brought in senior operations talent at plant level to negotiate these long-term contracts and dynamically rebalance launch schedules against available component capacity.
supplier LTAs targeted for FY2028 and FY2029; vertical integration under consideration in one case

Capacity ceiling stated: with the capex already deployed and the facilities and rooftops it has in place today, Modine believes the range is 'right around $4 billion' of revenue it can support over time. Going beyond that would require a different level of capex outlay, or a combination of an incremental facility, more efficiency on existing lines, and leveraging the supply chain to produce overflow capacity; design work is moving toward a more modular systems approach in the factory to add flexibility. The remaining chiller lines in Grenada, Jefferson City and the Dallas area are expected to be up and established at some level of efficiency by the end of the fiscal year. Coils production has been consolidated into Grenada and Juarez to allow the Grenada chiller lines to expand while preserving coil capacity for data-center customers; Heat Transfer Solutions sales improved 7%, or $11 million, on strong North America coil volume supporting data-center customers.
~$4 billion of revenue capacity on current capex and footprint; Grenada, Jefferson City and Dallas chiller lines running by end of fiscal 2027; coil sales +7% / $11M on data-center demand

Modine's 10-Q: Data Centers segment operating income was $46.3 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026 versus $34.7 million a year earlier. Data Centers cost of sales rose $149.3 million, or 116 percent, on higher sales volume, approximately $16.0 million of higher material costs, expenses of the rapid U.S. manufacturing capacity expansion, and supplier capacity constraints for certain key components that temporarily disrupted production schedules; Modine is working with current partners and qualifying additional suppliers to secure supply. Data Centers capital expenditures were $30.9 million versus $7.1 million, driven by investments to increase production capacity.

Data Centers operating income $46.3 million vs $34.7 million; Data Centers cost of sales +$149.3 million (+116 percent), material costs +~$16.0 million; Data Centers capex $30.9 million vs $7.1 million

Multilayer circuit board materials (MEGTRON): responding to strong demand, Panasonic is strengthening the supply chain including MULTI-SOURCING of key raw materials like glass cloth, in addition to building new production plants - capacity expansion for circuit board materials at Ayutthaya and Sukhothai sites; management concedes production capacity expansion was the challenge and 'we converted the phase completely'. For conductive polymer capacitors, plans to expand capacity at manufacturing sites are being accelerated; capex for capacitors and electronic materials being implemented EARLIER than the original plan because demand is growing faster than anticipated. Competitive backdrop: Taiwanese players are aggressively expanding capacity in circuit-board materials and capacitors; Panasonic cites high product capability (technical leadership in MEGTRON and capacitors). Supercapacitors attracting increased attention on surging AI server power consumption - mass production of devices for external customers to start at the Chitose plant during FY2027.
MEGTRON capacity expansion at Ayutthaya/Sukhothai + glass cloth multi-sourcing; capacitor capex pulled forward; Chitose supercapacitor mass production in FY2027

Raw materials and pricing: raw material/logistics prices a negative JPY 37 billion in Q1 (copper, resin and memory price hikes) and a negative JPY 66 billion expected for the full year - 'difficult to find the materials of which prices are not increasing': oil-linked resin, memories, metals (copper, silver), and device-specific tantalum and glass cloth, across essentially all segments. Price revisions/rationalization a positive JPY 54 billion in Q1 and JPY 59.6 billion expected full-year: Panasonic is raising prices not only to pass through material costs but also to lift unit prices and margins in high-demand AI-related materials and peripherals where supply is tight.
Raw material headwind JPY 66 billion FY (copper/resin/memory/tantalum/glass cloth); price revisions +JPY 59.6 billion FY

Craft labour is NOT the binding constraint today - Duke Austin: 'We're nowhere near capacity.' More than 85,000 employees; roughly 15,500 people added over the past year, well over 7,000 of them organic with a significant portion in Q2; Quanta spends about $250 million a year on training. It takes about four years to make a craftsman and a journeyman, and he sees no oversupply of craft-skilled labour in the near future. Labour is fungible across segments - electricians and underground crews move between data-center work, industrial and gas compression work and T&D - which is where the acquisition synergies show up. Customers are securing craft as far out as their five- to seven-year capital plans, with 'decade-plus type arrangements out there'. Margin follows that utilisation: the electric segment can operate at 10% to 12% on the utility side, with 12% the utmost 'when you stack in large transmission and all aspects at once', and Duke sees room for further margin improvement in the second half.
85,000+ employees, +15,500 over the year (>7,000 organic); ~$250M/yr training; 'nowhere near capacity'; electric segment margin range 10%-12% on the utility side

VERTICAL INTEGRATION INTO CRITICAL-PATH EQUIPMENT. Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' The rule he states: 'Anywhere there's a critical path that we think we can invest capital to move it forward, that's what you've seen us do... we're taking advantage of areas where there's underinvestment', and those vertical supply-chain investments are 'showing up in synergies'. He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Done collaboratively with the client it takes total installed cost down significantly and de-risks logistics; the Phalcon acquisition puts that capacity in the Northeast, close to where the work is.
HICO high-voltage breaker JV plus owned transformer and utility-pole manufacturing; fabrication footprint ~seven million sq ft, +0.5 million sq ft from the recent acquisitions

WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.
no specific figure (engine orders placed today carry a five- to six-year lead time; substation interconnection queue is the constraint)

Supply chain: SPX engineers its own fans, gear reducers and heat exchangers, giving it flexibility to build in-house or use third parties; before taking any large data-center order its supply chain team scrubs every bill-of-material item to validate it can deliver, having watched competitors fall down on supply chain. Management notes some customer concentration among a small number of hyperscalers.

Inventories at chip manufacturers in memory and logic had largely normalised, and Siltronic now sees indications that memory players are starting to rebuild wafer safety stocks, most likely to secure supply in an environment of strong AI-driven demand and tightening wafer availability; management called this safety-stock rebuilding a potential additional upside to wafer demand.

CEO Michael Heckmeier: customers are approaching Siltronic to manifest and confirm midterm demand, particularly in the memory space, where customers want to talk about volume developments two to three years out and discussions about new long-term agreements are starting; Siltronic engages but repeats that prices must come up to justify further investment.

300-millimeter demand recovery is becoming increasingly evident: new and smaller customers are approaching Siltronic and some existing customers are looking for upside volumes above their long-term agreement levels, which helped drive the Q2 sales improvement and the raised full-year sales guidance; management says it stays very careful and selective about whom it gives which volumes because the price level is still too low.

Balance sheet at end-June: total assets EUR 4.9 billion versus EUR 4.8 billion at year-end 2025, fixed assets down EUR 93 million as depreciation exceeded capex, cash and securities up to EUR 650 million on the capital increase, equity EUR 2.2 billion for an equity ratio of 45% versus 43% at year-end 2025, net financial debt down to EUR 692 million, plus an undrawn syndicated loan facility of EUR 127 million. Inventories rose on a targeted build to support improving demand and prepare for higher shipment volumes.
total assets EUR 4.9 billion; cash and securities EUR 650 million; equity EUR 2.2 billion; equity ratio 45%; net financial debt EUR 692 million; undrawn facility EUR 127 million

Utilisation is strong, particularly in the legacy fabs, and overall industry utilisation looks very high; equipment is still flowing into FabNext so capacity and output are still growing there, which is also why capex still runs ahead of the cash number. Lead times for further brownfield equipment are 18-24 months and Siltronic is in close contact with its major suppliers but has not triggered any future capex; no new greenfield fab will be announced anytime soon.

300-millimeter pricing: positive price developments are visible on low volumes in the non-LTA space, but spot pricing is still below the LTA price level and clearly below the reinvest level. CEO Michael Heckmeier: 'We always said prices need to come up and to cross the reinvest level. That holds true unchangeably.' Siltronic still expects an overall negative price impact for 2026 and will not commit to further brownfield investment or new long-term agreements until prices cross the reinvest level.

Around two-thirds of Siltronic's business is under long-term agreements, the majority of that in 300-millimeter, with one-third outside LTAs. Management sees no LTA cliff or major LTA change in 2027 or 2028; the major LTAs signed around 2020-2021 to underwrite FabNext run far beyond three years and some run until 2030, while a portfolio of shorter one-to-three-year agreements rolls over and could be renegotiated under better commercial terms in 2027 and 2028 if pricing improves.
around two-thirds of business under LTAs (majority 300mm); some LTAs run until 2030; no LTA cliff in 2027 or 2028

2026 wafer area consumption is still expected to grow by around 7% before inventory effects, unchanged from the Q1 view, but the mix outside servers weakened: smartphones now seen down around 11% and PCs down around 10%, automotive broadly unchanged at moderate growth of around 3%, and industrial applications up around 13% from a relatively low base including demand from data-center infrastructure.
wafer area consumption +7% in 2026; smartphones -11%; PCs -10%; automotive +3%; industrial +13%

On the wafer supply-demand balance, CEO Michael Heckmeier said there still seems to be a bit more wafer supply than demand, but that this could change pretty soon in the next quarters, with the price pattern the true indicator; a broad, meaningful wafer price increase has not happened yet, only small volumes here and there, and he argued a very significant price increase must come to the wafer industry to rebalance value creation across the chain.

Recent news flow from a competitor could create another smaller shortage in certain 200-millimeter products; some customers have approached Siltronic to fill that demand and some have even started discussions about 200-millimeter long-term agreements. Siltronic receives 200-millimeter requests from all over the globe including China, where customers want advanced specifications from the established supply base. Siltronic is restaffing lines it had been running on a cost- and cash-optimised basis to follow the demand.

GENERATION BUILDOUT FOR AI LOAD - 10 GW APPROVED AND GEORGIA ALREADY OVERSUBSCRIBED. Over the past several years Southern has secured regulatory approvals for 10 GW of new company-owned generation resources, including thermal, battery and solar, as well as hundreds of miles of new transmission lines. The first two of several battery sites are in service, and work on three combustion turbines at Plant Yates is advancing toward completion in the coming quarters. Poroch said the company is 'about 1 GW or 2 away from... selling out the capacity that we had approved in Georgia last year', and Womack added that 'the OpenAI contract in Georgia pushes us beyond our recently approved capacity by right around 1 GW' - i.e. the signed AI load has already outrun approved supply.
10 GW of new company-owned generation approved (thermal/battery/solar) + hundreds of miles of transmission; Georgia capacity ~1 GW oversubscribed after the OpenAI contract

NEW NUCLEAR: HYPERSCALERS BEING ASKED TO SHARE AP1000 COST-OVERRUN RISK. Womack said the country needs more nuclear units in operation particularly in the mid-2030s, credited the administration for regulatory actions and for convening groups around long-lead-time items, but stated plainly that 'Southern Company is not going to be next' on a new nuclear build. Asked whether hyperscalers are willing to absorb cost overruns above budgeted amounts for AP1000s, he said he did not want to get ahead of a firm conclusion but 'yes, we are having conversations with them in terms of what role they can play.'

Thailand ramp and inventory: Thailand plant phase 2 mass production slipped about two months on equipment-delivery delays, but phase-1 experience shortened the ramp curve - it began contributing shipments in July 2026, ramps through August, should help Q3 results and reach full output by Q4 2026. Inventory stands at NT$100 hundred million with turnover days down to 90 despite much higher revenue; management says inventory must keep rising as new capacity opens.
Thailand phase 2 contributing from July 2026, full output by Q4; inventory NT$100 hundred million, 90 turnover days

Management says demand is outstripping supply across the electrical value chain: 'the constraint is power and labor' - power is the ultimate largest governor of data center construction, followed by construction labor, with a variety of in-front-of-the-meter and behind-the-meter power solutions being worked; Wesco says it is not yet seeing data center demand crowd out its own non-residential construction business, which grew high-single-digit

Pricing on electrical gear is back to business as usual: an approximately 3% overall price benefit in the quarter split CSS +1%, EES +5% (about a point of that commodity driven) and UBS +3%; supplier partners are being 'very measured' about price with nothing out of the ordinary to highlight
price +~3% overall; CSS +1%, EES +5% (~1pt commodity), UBS +3%

Capacity utilization at 60% at the end of Q2, targeting a gradual increase toward 85%-90%; enough capacity in hand for the next two to three years under current growth projections; watching wafer supply tension closely — high demand for SOI wafers and 200 millimeter wafers, with any input price increases to be propagated to customers case by case

Supply chain and EPC capacity lock-in: over the past 3 to 4 years Xcel shifted to being a 'partner of choice' with its Tier 1 suppliers and EPC partners across a 5-plus year portfolio of nearly 13 gigawatts of new renewable generation and battery storage, over 3 gigawatts of new natural gas generation and nearly 2,000 high-voltage transmission line miles. Management said these partnerships 'help ensure that we have access to the labor and equipment capacity that we need to deliver with certainty for our customers well into the 2030s', supported by standardized repeatable designs and one consolidated project execution organization. Van Abel separately framed the build as 15-plus gigawatts of new generation.
nearly 13 GW renewables + storage, over 3 GW new natural gas, nearly 2,000 high-voltage transmission line miles under multi-year supplier/EPC agreements

Q3 2026 revenue guided to $630 million to $690 million, at midpoint up 4.8% QoQ and 46.3% YoY, exceeding market consensus despite longer lead times for certain materials; Q3 bookings expected to grow a high single-digit percentage sequentially, mainly driven by TCB and photonics; group gross margin expected to stay above 40% through Q3 and about three quarters out; full-year 2026 revenue growth expected across both SEMI and SMT.
Q3 revenue $630 million to $690 million (midpoint +4.8% QoQ, +46.3% YoY); group gross margin above 40%

Given the recent surge in demand, Advantest is accelerating capacity expansion efforts and pulling forward its original plans - going beyond increasing production volumes to strengthening the entire supply chain, deepening collaboration with production partners, securing critical components, maintaining quality, and ensuring timely delivery to customers.
Capacity expansion accelerated and original plans pulled forward; no specific figure

Generation equipment secured: 'about 7.5 GW of plant island equipment' (gas turbine power islands under contract with exclusivity), which is the low end of the 10 to 17 GW opportunity; no additional turbines added since Investor Day but the company is 'staying ahead' as the front end of the funnel fills. Cottonwood plant acquisition pending as the most economic option for near-term industrial (steel, LNG, petrochemical) load; a new plant would not be available until the early part of the next decade.
7.5 GW plant island equipment contracted (10-17 GW opportunity)

Capacity: 52 major projects underway across 33 markets (new projects announced in Chicago, Istanbul and Johor; opened Madrid, Milan and Silicon Valley); 3 GW of land under control with about 700 MW being built now, power either contracted or with a very high degree of confidence; a typical Equinix build is about 60 MW. Q2 CapEx about $1.6 billion, ~90% for capacity expansion. M&E pre-purchased where appropriate with a fungible design so equipment can move across the footprint.
52 major projects in 33 markets; 3 GW land under control, ~700 MW under construction; typical build ~60 MW; Q2 CapEx ~$1.6B

Record 9,700 net interconnection adds; 4,200 net cabinet billings; interconnection revenue growing around 9%; Cloud Router bookings +170% YoY; Fabric Geo Zones sovereignty product in preview with approximately 80 enterprises (from 20 last quarter); churn 1.8%, expected near the low end of the 2-2.5% range in 2H. Deal density is moving up as customers lock in capacity; per-kW pricing firm with meaningful mark-to-market opportunity in constrained metros such as Frankfurt, Amsterdam and Ashburn.
record 9,700 net interconnection adds; 4,200 net cabinet billings; Cloud Router bookings +170%; churn 1.8%

Capacity build-out for the back-half CPI ramp: Q1 net capex was $235 million (approximately 3% of revenue) and FY2027 capex is guided to $1.5-$1.6 billion, described as 'pretty significant investment in terms of facilities, cooling infrastructure, manufacturing infrastructure', most of it serving the FY2027 and FY2028 acceleration. CEO on constraints: 'Don't see any significant constraints per se other than putting the capacity investments in place and making sure those factories are ramped up' — the investments 'have been going on for a bit', not started 90 days ago.
Q1 capex $235M (~3% of revenue); FY27 capex $1.5-1.6B for CPI facilities/cooling capacity

High-voltage transition update: 'first is on 400 volt, which is kind of the immediate programs that we are working on, followed by 800 volt. We feel very good about the progress on those programs. Don't see any major limitations, at least to the guide we have given for 2027 and 2028', with solid-state transformer technology 'that is going to be coming our way' after that. CEO: 'Flex is kind of the leader in this transition on the embedded power side'. On components: 'there's lots of conversations about component constraints and all of that, we have planned all of that in the guide we have given. If anything, there should be some upside to that... as availability becomes better.' Updated long-term guidance around the transition comes at the November Investor Day.
400V programs ramping now, 800V next, solid-state after; component constraints already planned into the guide

Modular power capacity expansion in the US: 'we added capacity in Dallas after our Crown acquisition. Now with EP Squared acquisition, we're adding capacity in Iowa to really continue to drive that modular power business.' Flex calls itself 'very mature' in modular power deployment for both the utility and data-center spaces, and says demand exceeds supply: 'we're fighting against capacity constraints in that space to do more of it. It's the direction everyone is heading... because it's just so much easier to pick it up and deploy it at the customer site.'

CALL-ONLY / THE DDR SNAP-BACK, SEEN FROM THE PROBE-CARD SIDE: Q3 DRAM revenue is guided COMPARABLE to the record Q2 'but with a significant underlying SHIFT FROM HBM TO DDR'. The reason is the memory shortage itself - 'as you've heard recently from all our major DRAM customers, the supply environment continues to be EXTREMELY CONSTRAINED, and our customers are shifting their WAFER START MIX TO DDR DESIGNS to capture the profit opportunity provided by significant DDR PRICE INCREASES'. Because probe cards are specific to each customer chip design, FormFactor's mix tracks those wafer-start shifts one-for-one - making its DRAM mix a near-real-time proxy for where DRAM makers are actually pointing capacity 'while these unusual end market conditions persist'.
Q3 DRAM flat QoQ but mix shifts HBM -> DDR as makers chase DDR pricing

CALL-ONLY / THE MOST QUOTABLE SUPPLY TESTIMONY OF THE QUARTER: 'the industry now is probably operating very similar to what was in the PANDEMIC. EVERYTHING IS AT 100% UTILIZATION. Everything. CALL-ONLY / MEMORY DEMAND DESTRUCTION, NOW QUANTIFIED AND DATED. The handset market is expected DOWN LOW TEENS in 2026 versus 2025 with 'a lot of the impact in the LOWER TIERS'; QCT Android revenue is down 20% YoY and the EPS impact is 'GREATER THAN $1.50' - management explicitly frames that $1.50+ as a future TAILWIND once memory conditions normalize and agentic-AI handsets drive replacement. Timing call: Chinese-OEM handset revenue 'reached a BOTTOM in the third fiscal quarter and will return to DOUBLE-DIGIT SEQUENTIAL GROWTH in the fourth' - the mechanism being that OEMs had been under-buying against end demand while draining channel inventory, and 'the channel inventories has thinned down that they can't draw down anymore', so purchases now reconcile to the true market size. Handset market -low-teens 2026; QCT Android rev -20% YoY = >$1.50 EPS drag; China bottomed in FQ3; Apple share materially below 20%, ~-50% QoQ in Dec

NAND/DRAM scarcity is the defining constraint. NAND makers are redirecting focus and CapEx to DRAM and HBM, deemphasising eMMC/UFS and exiting automotive - which hands share to Silicon Motion's module-maker customers and gives it stronger pricing power. NAND scarcity expected to persist until 2028; DRAM+NAND ~56% of low-end smartphone BOM; smartphone units -10% to -15% in 2026

Management endorsed as 'a fair characterization' the view that high-capacitance MLCC demand ramping alongside next-generation AI servers will force conversion of mid/low-end capacity and put shortage pressure on the rest of the portfolio - part of its customer conversations already cover securing that non-AI piece too, with peers also raising MLCC utilization. Adjacent driver: the whole AI power chain 'from the grid down to the rack of the server' has many voltage step-down/conversion stages needing filtering and ripple-current management, driving strong growth in film capacitors and aluminum electrolytic capacitors plus the magnetics (inductors) and connector lines - embedded across computing, industrial and telecom segments. In notebooks, new tantalum packaging offering higher capacitance in a smaller package positions a laptop recovery as more of a 2027 story.

Carrier is fully booked for the second half; customers are pushing to accelerate deliveries rather than push them into 2027, and management sees no double-ordering risk because it is delivering into a rotable pool under strategic relationships in which hyperscalers and colos have established the share they expect to give Carrier. Cost per megawatt has risen versus the CoreWeave sites, where labour and equipment were secured starting in early 2024. On demand, management says data center capacity is still in very short supply and that large-scale GPU contracts are being signed today whose GPUs 'do not have a home yet', with a lot of GPUs sitting on the ground after late deliveries across the industry, which should tighten data-center supply further.

Power development at Pecos: an analyst noted an ERCOT update due August 7 covering roughly 815 MW, and management confirmed about 300 MW of that is the on-grid load study for Pecos with the rest behind-the-meter; given the uncertainty on the timing of that next 300 MW of on-grid power, the next megawatts at Pecos will be driven by the behind-the-meter strategy. Core Scientific is in advanced conversations with natural gas suppliers, has done preliminary planning on lateral pipeline development to the Pecos and Muskogee sites, and has held integrated conversations with on-site generation equipment providers - evaluating turbines, reciprocating engines, linear generators and fuel cells, with the technology choice varying by site geography, environmental conditions and supply-chain availability. The critical path per site is either the time to build the lateral pipeline or generation equipment manufacturing and production capacity. Capital was released for substation construction earlier this year across multiple sites, other sites are pad-ready for utility energization, and the full shell for the first 185 MW at Pecos will be complete within weeks.
~815 MW pending the ERCOT update (~300 MW on-grid load study at Pecos); 185 MW first shell at Pecos

US INDIUM PHOSPHIDE AND OPTICAL CAPACITY BUILD-OUT ACROSS THREE SITES — explicitly framed against 'the supply constraints in the market today'. (1) SAN JOSE: the new indium phosphide fab is now PROCESSING TEST WAFERS as it moves toward product qualification, and remains ON TRACK FOR VOLUME PRODUCTION BY THE END OF 2026. (2) PENNSYLVANIA: a June commitment to scale the facility, increasing ADVANCED TEST AND PACKAGING capacity for optical systems there BY 10 TIMES. (3) ARIZONA: announced on this call, Nokia is ACQUIRING A MANUFACTURING SITE FROM NXP where it plans to increase indium phosphide fab capacity, giving 'additional capacity to support our own demand and greater optionality'. Together these are described as strengthening and securing US-based optical manufacturing capacity for the long term. Nokia is vertically integrating InP at the same time merchant suppliers report InP demand outpacing supply.
San Jose InP fab volume production by end-2026; Pennsylvania test/packaging 10x; NXP Arizona site acquired for InP

Q2 2026 (ended 06-27-2026): net revenues $3.49B, above the midpoint of guidance, driven by Communication Equipment, Computer Peripherals and Automotive; gross margin 34.8% (non-GAAP 35.2%, +130bps YoY on lower unused-capacity charges and better mix, including ~60bps of non-recurring manufacturing-reshaping cost); non-GAAP diluted EPS $0.31; free cash flow +$75M; net financial position $2.01B. DEMAND INFLECTION: bookings strong with BOOK-TO-BILL CLOSE TO 2 OVERALL — above 1 in every end market and SIGNIFICANTLY ABOVE 2 in Communication Equipment & Computer Peripherals, 'mostly driven by optical connectivity, including silicon photonics' — with improved visibility and 'signs of TIGHT SUPPLY in several product categories'; distribution inventory now BELOW standard target. YoY by end market: Comms Equipment & Computer Peripherals +50%, Industrial +34%, Personal Electronics +20%, Automotive +16%. By segment YoY: Analog/MEMS/Sensors +26%, Embedded Processing +35.5%, RF & Optical +32%, Power & Discrete +3.7%. Q3 2026 guide: revenue $3.7B +/-350bps (+6.2% QoQ, +16.2% YoY) with gross margin ~37% (+/-200bps, incl ~70bps unused capacity). Q4 revenue expected ABOVE $4B — 'a revenue growth acceleration, mainly driven by our engaged customer programs in AI DATA CENTERS and LOW EARTH ORBIT satellite communication' — putting H2-over-H1 growth above the normal 15% seasonality.
Q2 rev $3.49B, GM 34.8%; book-to-bill ~2 (>2 in comms/peripherals); Q3 $3.7B, Q4 >$4B

→ Soitec: Shin-Etsu Handotai named as one of Soitec's wafer partners on input costs; Soitec says the supplier situation is tense but manageable, with a diversified supplier base and contribution (selling price minus raw material prices) improving slightly this year

More than 10 Photonic SOI customers, with multi-year capacity reservation agreements negotiated with most of them, including agreed prices, down payments or deposits, and visibility on customer inventory; commitments now extend beyond fiscal year 2027
more than 10 customers in Photonic SOI; multi-year commitments extending beyond FY2027

Singapore 300-millimeter SOI fab qualified for high-volume Photonic SOI manufacturing with first customers, accelerated from an initial end-of-calendar-year plan; no bottleneck — 'lead time to peak' rather than a capacity limit, leveraging fungibility across SOI products; V4 module expansion starting in Bernin and the Singapore building can be equipped further; Q1 average fab loading 48% (down from 74% a year earlier on inventory reduction), around 65% average expected for the year
Q1 fab loading 48% vs 74% a year earlier; ~65% average loading expected for the year

CFO on equipment procurement: "we've proactively secured supply to support both FPL and Energy Resources development plans, including the development of our national data center hub footprint. For solar, we've secured panels through 2029. We're also well protected for battery storage with competitively priced domestic supply also secured through 2029. We have sufficient wind sites with expected federal permits to meet development expectations through 2029. And we have sufficient transformer capacity to support our build forecast through the end of the decade." Framed as planning for potential trade impacts. No equipment supplier was named on the call.
solar panels secured through 2029; domestic battery storage supply secured through 2029; wind sites/permits through 2029; transformer capacity secured through the end of the decade

Production growth is supply-chain limited, not demand limited: 'Production growth will be limited by our supply chain. This includes not just batteries, but also ELECTRONIC COMPONENTS... our Tesla team is working actively to unblock the obstacles ahead by securing strategic deals with suppliers' (CFO Vaibhav Taneja). Musk separately described 'the pretty insane pricing of memory these days' and said memory suppliers are having to make 'very tough decisions on memory allocation'.

Optimus supply chain has to be built or in-sourced: 'with Optimus, there is no supply chain. So we've had to build up the supply chain in its entirety or in-house the production.' Optimus power electronics and circuit boards are all Tesla-designed but fabricated by suppliers today; OPTIMUS 4, to be built in Austin, will be much more vertically integrated (PCB work brought in-house), with an aspirational 10 MILLION UNITS A YEAR versus 1 MILLION UNITS A YEAR for Optimus 3. VP of Supply Chain Karn Budhiraj: supplier investment at the same scale is 'going to memory and also new specific like metal injection molded parts, flexible printed circuits and all sorts of nonlinear technologies that are more based for the robot as opposed to the traditional vehicle supply chain', and Tesla in-sources where no good partner is found.
Optimus 4 aspiration ~10 million units a year vs ~1 million units a year for Optimus 3

Capacity is the constraint on converting record orders: most load factors are 'really high' — to a level that becomes less productive (air shipments to manage lead times); Energy Division margin dented by slight negative mix, provisions/reserves, inflation, currency and uneven load in some units (Welded, Cryo — Cryo quickly resolved by the Q2 order book). Data-center demands to scale are high: current CapEx levels kept in the MEDIUM TERM to support customer agreements PAST 2027 — full-year CapEx SEK 2.5 billion-SEK 3 billion, expected to remain at that level a couple of years; capacity increases coming online in this year and importantly beginning of 2027 are already essentially fully booked, and NEW capacity investment decisions are being made now against underlying 2028+ demand. US fluid-handling capacity from investments a year/year-and-a-half ago now coming online.
FY CapEx SEK 2.5 billion-SEK 3 billion, staying elevated a couple of years; 2027 capacity additions essentially fully booked

Q2 2026 (ended 06-30-2026): product+royalty revenue $143.4M (+26.9% QoQ, +1.6% YoY vs a year-ago quarter that included a $45M patent-litigation settlement); advanced products $94.2M (+45% QoQ, 65.7% of revenue); brick $49.2M; gross margin 58% (+280bps QoQ); net income $49.8M, diluted EPS figure garbled in the call transcript (a dropped zero; the filed figure is on the Vicor 8-K entry), helped by a $10.9M tax benefit; cash $453.6M (+$49.4M); received $14.3M CHIPS Act investment tax credit refund from the IRS (07-13-2026, from 2023 return, more expected). One-year backlog +26% QoQ to $379.7M, book-to-bill above 1. Guidance: Q3 revenue +~10% QoQ, FY2026 >$600M (raised from ~$570M) with double-digit sequential advanced-product growth; margin expansion expected. Lead times stretching industry-wide — 'demand exceeding capacity in a number of key areas'.
Q2 rev $143.4M (+26.9% QoQ); backlog $379.7M (+26%); FY guide >$600M

Supply chain constraints are the bottleneck, not demand: market-wide crunch in FANS plus valves and certain components; the setup of a localized US bill of material was delayed, forcing continued shipment of components from Europe into the US — tariff impact in the quarter was 3% (imports of finished goods from Italian production and chiller components from Europe). Ramp-up is about ONE QUARTER BEHIND plan. Factory build itself is on track: Virginia facility production output DOUBLED and floor space increased 60%. Mitigation: qualifying new fan suppliers, pre-ordering/building stock, organizing supply outside North America; no delivery delays to customers expected (product-mix shifts across the wide portfolio), no signs of customer dissatisfaction or share loss to competitors.
Tariff impact 3%; ramp one quarter behind plan; Virginia output doubled, floor space +60%

Capacity is the governor of order intake: 'We do not take orders where we aren't fully committed that we can deliver on time.' Guidance raised because capacity from previous years' investments is now coming online with the expected benefits; multi-year CapEx build-out across the US, China and India, plus a newly announced $200 million expansion and additional CapEx into Europe. Continuous expansion 'especially in Electrification, every unit that we have with more square meter, more Robotics, more Automation and more people'. Lead times unchanged — order strength reflects real demand, not lead-time extension or pre-buying.
$200 million additional European capacity CapEx announced; capacity additions in US, China, India

MEMORY-RELATED NET SYSTEM SALES NOW GUIDED TO GROW OVER 75% IN 2026 — memory was 49% of Q2 net system sales (EUR 6.6B total). Driver per CEO Christophe Fouquet: 'the supply challenges driving up both DDR AND HBM PRICES have prompted significant investments in fab expansion', with customers adding meaningful capacity this year AND planning MULTIPLE MEGA FABS that come online in phases over the coming years. Growth is a combination of (1) much higher VOLUME for both HBM and DDR — 'HBM will require more wafer, there's a volume effect' — with some product mix shifting toward DDR on very strong DDR pricing, and (2) rising LITHO INTENSITY as customers migrate to advanced nodes: the 1c node ('going to be enormous') and 1b use more EUV layers, with Low-NA EUV growth driven by replacing multi-patterning with more cost-effective SINGLE-EXPOSE EUV, plus more immersion DUV. Fouquet: 'this combination which create a bit the perfect storm for ASML on DRAM this year and most probably the next few years to come.' Company-wide: Q2 net sales EUR 9.3B above guidance, FY2026 raised to EUR 43-45B; ~65 Low-NA EUV systems shipping in 2026 with 2027 Low-NA EUV nearly sold out and capacity being raised ~30%.
FY26 memory system sales +>75%; memory 49% of Q2 systems; 1c/1b add EUV layers

CAPACITY EXPANSION on multi-year customer visibility: order momentum 'extremely strong' through H1 with backlog increasing across a broad mix of customers. For 2027 ASML is now CLOSE TO FULLY COVERED WITH ORDERS FOR LOW-NA EUV and is planning to increase Low-NA EUV capacity by ~30%; for 2028 it has ALREADY RECEIVED A SIGNIFICANT NUMBER of Low-NA EUV orders (~two years in advance, a situation 'we haven't enjoyed in many years') and is investigating a FURTHER 30% increase (toward ~110 units). Immersion capacity to rise 30% in 2027 with a potential further 30% for 2028 under investigation. All of these increases are achievable WITHIN THE EXISTING CLEANROOM FOOTPRINT by optimizing existing space — no new cleanroom required. Pricing: value-based pricing gives 'more flexibility for pricing than what you would have seen in the past', though long order lead times delay the effect. Next Capital Markets Day 06-10-2027.
2027 Low-NA EUV nearly sold out, capacity +30%; 2028 +30% under study (~110 units)

OPTICAL IS NOW AEHR'S SECOND PILLAR: optical device test and burn-in for DATA CENTER INFRASTRUCTURE TRANSCEIVERS, CHIP-TO-CHIP I/O and hard disk drives accounted for approximately 20% OF FISCAL 2026 REVENUE, alongside AI accelerators/CPUs/network processors at ~71% — and management expects BOTH markets to grow significantly in fiscal 2027. Silicon photonics is named as one of the two focus areas (with AI accelerators) that together drove the majority of fourth-quarter revenue. Company-wide: record quarterly bookings, record effective backlog over $100M, and FY2027 revenue guided to $130-150M (2.6x-3x fiscal 2026) with 18-22% non-GAAP pretax margin and no capacity constraint at that level. Two years ago over 95% of Aehr's revenue was EV silicon carbide; today almost 95% comes from other markets.
Optical/data-centre device burn-in ~20% of FY26 revenue; silicon photonics a named growth driver

LEAD AI-PROCESSOR CUSTOMER SCALING: Aehr's lead AI-processor wafer-level burn-in customer is 'significantly ramping their products', driving increased forecast capacity needs for FOX systems and proprietary WaferPak full-wafer contactors; over the past year that customer ordered fully automated WAFERPAK ALIGNERS to integrate with its installed base, DOUBLED its systems from Aehr, and is forecasting significant increases in WAFER ALLOCATION FROM ITS FOUNDRY (previously a constraint on its growth). Critically, the customer MOVED ALL PRODUCTION BURN-IN SCREENING TO WAFER-LEVEL BURN-IN on Aehr's system and NO LONGER PERFORMS ANY SYSTEM-LEVEL SCREENING of those products — Aehr is described as 'a critical supplier'. Technology advantage cited: the WaferPak contactor manages INDIVIDUAL DIE TEMPERATURES, giving significantly better thermal management than conventional package-level approaches; systems process up to a quarter of a wafer at a time with as many as NINE WAFERS TESTED IN PARALLEL.
Lead AI customer doubled systems, moved ALL production burn-in to wafer level; 9 wafers in parallel

Supply tightness expected to persist over the next several quarters; DDR4/LPDDR4 supply is restricted — customers cannot get sufficient supply from other suppliers, and Nanya cannot support double-booking or pull-in requests; multi-year LTAs aligning supply and demand beyond 2028 (fixed volume+price renewed at term end, or committed volume with mostly quarterly market-based pricing)

Integrated Memory net sales were $275 million, up 111% year-over-year and 60% sequentially on both higher volume and pricing; the memory business is anchored on data center demand driven by agentic AI, with backlog growing as demand outpaces net sales; one memory customer is a hyperscaler buying memory modules for its data center product, though management says it is not a multi-hundred-million-dollar account.
memory net sales $275 million, +111% YoY, +60% QoQ

Exited Q3 with a very strong backlog; the bookings-to-revenue lag for the AI infrastructure business within Advanced Computing is 3 to 6 months, giving visibility into the first half of fiscal 2027; the outlook contemplates ongoing supply-chain constraints including extended lead times for certain components that affect how quickly new customer projects ramp, and industry-wide higher memory costs.

Q3 FY2026: AI-server input constraints persist - HBM in high demand with lead times extending; high-end high-density-interconnect PCBs in high demand; DDR4-and-below memory faces some shortages while DDR5 capacity is 'decent'; hyperscalers secure more than their fair share of constrained components. Jabil manages via access, allocation and long-term commitments rather than transactional pricing. Networking & communications grew >50% YoY (India ramp ~2x, InfiniBand/Ethernet) and capital/test-equipment demand was 'through the roof' on rapid chip-technology evolution (wafer-fab equipment recovering). Jabil contract-manufactures AI server/GPU PCBs populated with MLCCs and high-density interconnect.
HBM lead times extending; high-density-interconnect PCBs in high demand; DDR4 shortages, DDR5 decent

Supply-chain constraints are ALREADY BUILT INTO the preliminary FY2027 AI growth outlook — 'we're aware of where the shortages are... the numbers we talked about definitely have that built in'. Management is relatively relaxed on the AI side specifically because large Intelligent Infrastructure customers 'do manage to get their fair share and then some' of constrained components ('I don't lose that much sleep over it from the Intelligent Infrastructure standpoint'). The nature of supplier engagement has shifted: 'it's not transactional, it's not about pricing — it's about strategy, it's about access, it's about allocation, long-term commitments.'
FY27 outlook has shortages built in; AI customers get 'fair share and then some'

China substrate export licence still pending: VPEC has not yet received the export permit for substrates affected by China's export controls, but two weeks ago it was notified to file supplementary documents (routine paperwork) and completed the filing last week - management likens the situation to finally seeing the light at the end of the tunnel.

Capacity: Kulim (Malaysia) plant 1 successfully running high volume production of advanced substrates, with the next generation of larger advanced substrates under development; new customer-financed capacity expansion for AI-related substrates announced in Chongqing under a long-term contract (accretive from the start, high double-digit EUR million bottom-line impact); Leoben and Fehring in Austria being rebuilt for embedding of high-power electronics (partly single source) with revenue impact from the second half of the year; Shanghai focused on accelerator cards, co-packaged optics and embedded optics. T-glass shortage managed by expanding allocation from existing suppliers and qualifying new ones, though some effects remain on finished product availability; inflationary input cost increases (an ABF price increase was flagged by an analyst) are passed through to customers with a delay of a couple of months.

Momentum remains very strong and management is optimistic 2026 revenue keeps setting records, with the second half stronger than the first. In DIY motherboards and graphics cards, memory price hikes and CPU shortages have buyers waiting - ASPs are rising while mid-range unit volumes dip, but high-end demand is intact; the demand is seen as delayed rather than lost, and the H2 peak season is still expected, helped by added AI-compute demand, even as research firms forecast global PC shipments to fall this year. Full-year capex is estimated around NT$25-27 hundred million (Q1: NT$4.8 hundred million), mostly office building and production equipment.
2026 capex about NT$25-27 hundred million (Q1 NT$4.8 hundred million)

Board-level components are the shortage zone: power ICs are short, and passives (MLCC-type components) and PCB also show shortages, driven by overall market demand rather than any single product, so Inventec is pre-buying materials. Memory, hard drives and SSD are customer-controlled buy-and-sell items, so customers bear those materials while Inventec is responsible for board-level components.

Capacity and cost dynamics: Legrand has scaled with US data-center demand WITHOUT materially changing its CapEx-to-sales ratio of about 2% — 'data center is not a CapEx-intensive industry' for Legrand — absorbing ramp inefficiencies (air freight, subcontracting, overtime) without significant P&L impact. Gross margin down 190 basis points as pricing of +2.3% did not yet compensate inflation of +4.2% on raw materials/components and +3% on personnel cost (half of the ~4% purchase-price increase is tariff effect); gap expected to ease through the year. Four acquisitions announced so far in 2026, all in data centers and energy transition, representing combined annual revenue of around EUR 275 million.
CapEx ~2% of sales maintained; pricing +2.3% vs raw-material inflation +4.2%; four 2026 acquisitions ~EUR 275 million combined revenue

Strong 300mm wafer demand from leading-edge DRAM for AI data centers is a core part of SUMCO's outlook; memory makers' supply constraints are so tight they are curbing wafer demand from NON-leading-edge logic customers (memory shortage spillover). Long-term contract prices maintained.
leading-edge DRAM wafer demand strong; memory shortage spillover

Wafer market outlook: semiconductor market sees continued strong AI growth and only gradual recovery elsewhere. 300mm demand strong for leading-edge logic and DRAM in AI data centers with a projected NAND uptick ahead; recovery in non-leading-edge logic is gradual and partly TEMPERED BY MEMORY SHORTAGES (memory supply constraints curb non-leading-edge logic demand). 200mm and smaller lacks momentum, inventory-adjustment progress varies by customer.
AI leading-edge strong vs non-AI gradual; memory shortage caps non-leading-edge logic

US transformer market faces severe supply constraints with lead times extended to ~4 YEARS; a major factor is limited availability of grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) and copper — premium GOES is supplied by only a few producers (Nippon Steel, POSCO, Thyssenkrupp), supporting multi-year demand visibility for transformer-core steel into grid/datacenter expansion.
US transformer lead times ~4 years; GOES scarcity

Trainium2 has ~30% better price-performance than comparable GPUs and is largely SOLD OUT; a consistent majority of Bedrock inference workloads run on Trainium; delivered 4x improvement in Trainium2 token throughput during 2025.
Trainium2 ~30% better price-perf, largely sold out

Q1 2026: RECORD quarter — revenue, gross margin and operating income all MATERIALLY above prior outlook, revenue growth >100% YoY, record Q1 operating cash flow. Full-year guidance RAISED MATERIALLY (non-GAAP EPS now $1.85-2.25; FY2026 expected best in company history). Manufacturing footprint can deliver 5 GIGAWATTS of product annually — "not order constrained and not capacity constrained": revenue pace decided by how fast customers can deploy. Time-to-power has become "an existential necessity" for AI builders bumping into grid/permits/community bottlenecks.
Record Q1, rev >+100% YoY; FY EPS guide $1.85-2.25; 5GW/yr manufacturing capacity

The 2028 game changer: the biggest GPU vendor's next-generation GPU (2028) disclosed 3D stacking that is FORECAST TO BE HYBRID BONDED - equipment ordered in 2026, installed in 2027, volume production from 2028. BESI raised HB bonder capacity from ~15/month (~180/yr) to 250/YEAR, lead time ~6 months (100nm-accuracy tool), able to satisfy any model from "the big five". Long-term model: EUR 1.5-1.9B revenue in 3-5 years (~2.5-3x current) with the support infrastructure being built now; service revenue (15-16% of sales) to move toward 18-20% as the HB installed base adopts a front-end-style 24/7 support model (~900 defined spare parts, 4-hour availability) - a GROSS-MARGIN TAILWIND. Onshoring: TSMC/Amkor/Micron US advanced-packaging fabs build through 2026-27 with volume production from 2028 - BESI engaged in those programs.
Next-gen GPU 2028 = hybrid bonded (orders 2026); HB capacity to 250/yr; LT model EUR 1.5-1.9B

Data-center power positioning: competing in application-specific sockets — stage-one high-voltage conversion (800V down to 12V/6V) and stage-two VRM / final VCORE multiphase delivery for GPUs — built on 15 years of GaN investment plus advanced BCD nodes manufactured in Texas ('geopolitically dependable'); ASSP design-ins gaining momentum, expected to kick in H2 2026 and into 2027. Beyond ASSPs, an AI rack carries TENS OF THOUSANDS of general-purpose analog parts across many SKUs — TI claims it can fulfill almost every analog socket, and is winning sockets when competitors hit supply shortages.
800V->12/6V stage-1 + VRM stage-2 sockets; tens of thousands of GP analog parts per rack

Kinsus ABF substrate capacity has SOLD OUT (alongside Unimicron and Nan Ya PCB) on escalating AI chip demand; industry ABF quotes expected +5-10% QoQ from Q2 2026, spot prices +30%+; Taiwanese suppliers making AI-chip ABF expansion the primary 2026 capacity goal.
Kinsus ABF sold out; pricing rising

ABF substrate has SOLD OUT at Unimicron, Kinsus and Nan Ya PCB as AI chip demand escalates; ABF quotes expected +5-10% QoQ on average from Q2 2026 while spot prices are up >30%. March 2026 Nan Ya PCB revenue NT$4.29B (+39% YoY), a 36-month high.
ABF sold out; quotes +5-10% QoQ, spot +30%
Landmark commits to significant capacity expansion in 2026 to address light source supply tightness

InP substrate supply constraints (used in both EML and CW lasers, across PD receivers and LD transmitters), under geopolitical tension / export controls by China government; GS expects light source supply to remain tight through 2027
YJ Semi commits to significant capacity expansion in 2026 to address light source supply tightness

Memory is the biggest cost pressure for 2026: at current prices memory has reached about 30% of general-server cost (already factoring the recent sharp hikes; the share could exceed that if prices keep rising - management noted memory may have risen toward 4x), while the share in AI servers is smaller because GPU/ASIC content dominates. Customers held long-term contract prices last year so the 2025 increase felt moderate, but increases turned aggressive recently. Gross margin will be better than Q4 but is not expected to return to prior levels; the absolute profit impact is minimal-to-none because material is passed through - quotes separate material cost from Wiwynn's service fee. CSPs are signing long-term contracts and booking capacity with memory makers, and Wiwynn sees at least one quarter of secured supply with no material shortage for itself.
memory about 30% of general-server cost, already factoring recent hikes

10-K: Solstice's order rates have surpassed its existing production capacity for certain key product lines. Capital expenditures incurred were $408 million in 2025 (capital expenditures representing 10% of net sales) versus $296 million in 2024, and are expected to be between $400 million and $425 million in 2026; the increase in 2025 and expected 2026 capex is primarily driven by projects to support new products and solutions for its electronic materials and advanced fiber offerings. Electronic & Specialty Materials segment capex was $173 million in 2025 versus $63 million in 2024.
capex $408 million (2025) vs $296 million (2024); 2026 expected $400 million to $425 million; Electronic & Specialty Materials capex $173 million (2025) vs $63 million (2024)

capex expected at or above 10% of net sales in the near-term

AI test intensity is compounding because design margins are shrinking: higher data rates, lower latency and the requirement that AI fabrics be LOSSLESS mean customers 'can no longer guarantee anything by design' and must test in production too. A compute or switch tray has gone from tens to HUNDREDS of IC pinouts - more insertion points - tested at signal level (VNAs, oscilloscopes), at bit level (new portfolio) and at protocol/packet level (AI workload emulators). The move from monolithic chips to CHIPLET architectures adds interoperability emulation, and customers now ask for emulation environments that stress a chip while it exercises a model (thermal shutdown, all cores active at higher power and speed). The ecosystem is shifting from a homogeneous integrated vertical stack to a HETEROGENEOUS one - GPU/CPU/DPU mixes and a growing number of protocols at every layer of the stack - which broadens Keysight's addressable tail. The four wireline pillars (AI infrastructure scaling, speed transitions, silicon photonics, system-level emulation) all drove growth. Hyperscaler engagement (rooted in the Ixia acquisition ~5 years ago) is deepening as they integrate Keysight pre-silicon emulation and workload solutions into their development pipelines; hyperscalers plus the model companies are ~10% OF REVENUE DIRECTLY but drive large downstream influence, and many are building their own in-house silicon. Switch designers use Keysight emulators to validate network performance across AI workloads and protocols; interconnect manufacturers use high-fidelity analyzers to characterize high-speed backplanes for signal integrity and manufacturing yield.
